Competition in Generative AI: Evidence from Consumer Demand Mark L. Egan, Dominic Russel, Claire Shi, and Vincent Yao NBER Working Paper No. 35953 October 2026 JEL No. D12, L13, O33 ABSTRACT How competitive will the market for generative AI be as it matures? Using novel transaction level credit and debit card data covering 174 million consumers and 114 billion transactions, we study the adoption of paid services and the demand-side foundations of competition in this market. As of April 2026, approximately 2.9% of U.S. consumers pay for at least one major generative AI service, with adoption highest among younger and higher-income consumers. Nearly all of these paid users subscribe to basic plans that cost $30 or less per month. Three patterns suggest limited differentiation and low switching costs. First, although multihoming is common, it has declined as providers’ capabilities have expanded. Second, annual customer retention rates range from 20% to 45% across major AI providers, lower than those for many other subscription products. Third, switching rises around major model releases. Motivated by these findings, we develop and estimate a structural model of AI service demand and supply that reveals strong competitive pressure. Consumers are highly price sensitive, have much weaker preferences for particular providers than for AI overall, and view AI services as increasingly close substitutes. Our results suggest that, absent a substantial increase in AI model quality differentiation, growing substitutability among services will constrain providers’ pricing power and allow consumers to capture a large share of the surplus generated by these services. Mark L. Egan Harvard University Department of Economics and NBER megan@hbs.edu Dominic Russel Harvard University drussel@g.harvard.edu Claire Shi Harvard University cshi@g.harvard.edu Vincent Yao Georgia State University wyao2@gsu.edu

1 Introduction Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have the potential to transform economic activity and daily life. Since the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in late 2022 and Anthropic’s Claude in 2023, generative AI has rapidly become a prominent consumer technology used for a wide variety of everyday tasks, ranging from writing and coding to research and education. The adoption and pricing of these services, their effects on consumer welfare, and the valuations of AI firms will depend on how competitive the market becomes. A central question is therefore whether providers of consumer-facing generative AI services can sustain market power as the market matures. The answer depends in part on consumer demand, particularly on how differentiated consumers perceive services to be and how readily they substitute one service for another. Yet, despite generative AI’s rapid growth and economic importance, systematic evidence on consumer demand and competition remains limited. In particular, little is known about who pays for these services, how consumers choose among providers, how persistent paid subscriptions are, whether services are substitutes or complements, and how responsive consumers are to changes in price and quality . This paper uses novel, de-identified transaction-level credit and debit card data to study consumer adoption of and demand for paid generative AI services. We first document how adoption varies across demographic groups and regions and how it has evolved over time. We then examine purchasing dynamics, including how long paid subscriptions persist, what leads consumers to switch providers, and whether they multihome. These patterns shed light on the degree of differentiation among services and consumers’ willingness to substitute across them— two demand-side forces that are critical to understanding competition, consumer welfare, and the market’s long-run structure. Motivated by these empirical patterns, we develop and estimate a structural model of AI service demand and supply . The demand side of the model builds on Gentzkow (2007) and uses the panel structure of our data to separately identify consumers’ preferences for individual services, the correlation in those preferences across services, and the incremental utility from subscribing to multiple services. Distinguishing correlated preferences from complementarity is important. A consumer may subscribe to both OpenAI and Anthropic products because of a strong general taste for AI, or because they are complements so that subscribing to one raises the value of the other. These features of demand have distinct implications for competition. We use the estimated model to quantify how these forces shape market power, measure the surplus generated by AI services and its division between consumers and providers, and examine how changes in market structure affect competition. Overall, our reduced-form and structural results point to strong demand-side competitive pressure in the market for consumer AI services. Consumers differ substantially in their overall taste for AI, but provider-specific tastes are small relative to this common component: for instance, consumers who value an OpenAI product also tend to value an Anthropic product. Moreover, as model capabilities have expanded and converged, consumers increasingly treat these services as substitutes. Access to one service is therefore less valuable to a consumer who already has access to another. Together with consumers’ price sensitivity , these patterns leave providers with limited scope to sustain market power through provider-specific preferences. Although consumers’ sensitivity to model quality could give a provider market power if it achieves a level of quality that rivals cannot match, frontier model capabilities have thus far converged across providers. Absent a reversal of this pattern, our results suggest that the demand side is unlikely to support sustained market power and that, ultimately , consumers will capture a large share of the surplus generated by generative AI products. Our transaction-level sample spans January 2021 through April 2026 and contains 174 million consumers and 114 billion transactions. Transaction descriptors allow us to identify payments to major AI providers. We focus primarily on the four large generative AI providers observed in our data: Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), OpenAI (ChatGPT), and xAI (Grok). For each transaction, we observe the date and amount, together with anonymized identifiers for the card and consumer. These data allow us to construct a panel that tracks consumers’ purchases over time and across AI providers. We also observe demographic information, including consumers’ ages, incomes, and regions. We focus on paid consumer adoption, excluding both free AI subscriptions and enterprise adoption. Unlike free subscriptions, paid AI subscriptions reflect providers’ ability to monetize consumer demand, and are a core source of their revenue. For OpenAI, consumer subscriptions account for approximately 75% of revenue in 2024 and 60% at the beginning of 2026. Even Anthropic, which has traditionally targeted enterprise customers, generates approximately 20% of its revenue from consumer sales.1 Consumer subscriptions may also be especially important for future improvements in model quality , since AI companies generally do not train models on enterprise data. We use the data to document several new facts about consumer adoption of paid AI services. First, paid adoption has grown but remains relatively limited in the United States. In April 2026, 2.9% of consumers paid for at least one product from one of the four major AI providers in our sample, in line with recent industry estimates.2 OpenAI was the most widely adopted provider, with 2.4% of consumers paying for an OpenAI product. Although the share of consumers paying for Anthropic products had grown in recent months, it remained at only 0.5% in April 2026. Paid adoption is substantially more common among younger and higher-income consumers: those earning more than $200,000 per year are 1.7 times as likely to pay as those earning less than $50,000, and those younger than 55 are 1.8 times as likely as those aged 55 or older. These relationships between demographics and adoption hold broadly across AI providers. We also 1See estimates from Gavin (2026); Parham (2026); Lin (2025). 2See, for example, Bank of America Institute (2026); PNC Economics Research (2026). document meaningful geographic variation, with adoption highest in California, Washington, and the Mid-Atlantic region. Second, consumers frequently multihome across AI providers, particularly during the earlier part of our sample. For example, roughly 45% of consumers who paid for an Anthropic product also paid for an OpenAI product in June 2024. However, the prevalence of multihoming has declined over time. By April 2026, less than 30% of consumers who paid for an Anthropic product also paid for an OpenAI product. This decline is consistent with AI services becoming less complementary as providers have developed increasingly general-purpose products with overlapping capabilities. Third, retention among paying customers is low, especially relative to other subscription products such as newspapers and streaming services. We measure retention by following a consumer’s first observed purchase from an AI provider. Retention varies across providers and is highest for OpenAI: after 12 months, roughly 45% of OpenAI users remain subscribed, compared with 30% of Anthropic users. By comparison, annual retention rates for Netflix and Spotify in our data are around 70%. Fourth, consumers switch across providers, and switching activity increases following major model releases. We measure model capabilities using data from the Epoch Capabilities Index (Epoch AI, 2025). When Anthropic or OpenAI releases an improved model, the share of consumers who paid only for the rival in the previous month and begin paying for the provider with the model improvement rises by about 25%. Taken together, these facts describe a growing market characterized by limited customer loyalty and services that appear increasingly substitutable. If these patterns persist, they suggest that the market for AI services will likely be highly competitive and it will be challenging for providers to sustain market power in the long run. Motivated by these reduced-form facts, we develop and estimate a structural model of demand for AI services to better understand consumer preferences, how those preferences have evolved over time, the resulting welfare consequences, and the implications for market structure. Following Gentzkow (2007), we model consumer choice as a discrete-choice problem in which consumers choose among bundles of AI services rather than necessarily selecting a single service. The model allows consumers to purchase multiple services simultaneously and permits pairs of services to be either complements or substitutes. We allow consumers to have heterogeneous and correlated preferences across AI services in the spirit of Berryet al.(1995) and Berryet al.(2004). Distinguishing preference heterogeneity from complementarity is particularly important given that either force can explain the prevalence of multihoming. For example, a consumer who places a high value on Anthropic’s Claude may also place a high value on OpenAI’s ChatGPT because the consumer has a strong general preference for AI services, even if the two services are substitutes. Alternatively , the services may be complements, such that subscribing to Claude increases the value of subscribing to ChatGPT. On the supply side, we assume that AI providers compete in a differentiated-products Bertrand–Nash price-setting game. Providers recognize that consumers may purchase bundles containing products from multiple firms and that the price of one product can therefore affect demand for other products. When products are substitutes, a price increase by one provider shifts demand toward its competitors. When products are complements, a price increase can reduce demand for both products. Thus, greater substitutability intensifies price competition, whereas greater complementarity softens competition and supports higher equilibrium prices. We also consider a dynamic extension with learning by doing on the supply side. Specifically , we allow future model capabilities to depend on the number of users a provider attracts today , reflecting the idea that a larger user base gives the provider access to more data or resources that can be used to improve model quality (Prufer and Schottmüller, 2021; Hagiu and Wright, 2023). This force creates a dynamic incentive to set lower prices today: lower prices attract more users, improving future model quality and raising future demand. We estimate the demand model by maximum likelihood using our transaction-level panel data on consumer purchase decisions. The panel structure is central to separately identifying persistent heterogeneity in consumer preferences, correlations in preferences across providers, and complementarity or substitutability between AI services. Repeated purchase decisions and switching patterns identify persistent differences in consumers’ preferences. Correlated purchase behavior across providers helps identify correlations in preferences, while, conditional on those preferences, consumers’ tendency to multihome rather than switch between services helps identify whether the services are complements or substitutes. Our structural estimates on the demand side provide insight into the nature of consumer preferences and how they have evolved over time. To begin, consumer demand for AI services is relatively price elastic, with an average own-price elasticity of about -4.6. In our model, this high elasticity implies relatively little horizontal differentiation across AI providers and thus limited market power for providers. Our estimates of consumer preference heterogeneity reinforce the conclusion of limited horizontal differentiation. Although preferences vary substantially across consumers, consumerspecific preferences are strongly correlated across AI providers: consumers who value one provider more than average also tend to highly value other providers. For example, the estimated correlation between consumer-specific preferences for OpenAI and Anthropic products is 0.89. The lowest preference correlation between any pair of products is OpenAI and Google, at 0.55, which is still substantial. These estimates suggest that providers largely appeal to the same consumers and that provider-specific preferences account for relatively little of the variation in demand. Despite this limited horizontal differentiation, we find some degree of vertical differentiation across providers, consistent with observed market shares. At the end of our sample, the average consumer was willing to pay a $10 monthly premium for OpenAI products relative to Anthropic products. Part of this difference reflects model quality: our estimates indicate that consumers are willing to pay more for higher-quality models. For instance, moving from GPT- 4’s capability level to GPT-5.5 Pro’s raises average willingness to pay for OpenAI products by approximately $25 per month. Finally , we generally find that consumers increasingly view AI services as substitutes, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic products. As the capabilities of these services have expanded and converged, the incremental value of subscribing to one service for a consumer who already subscribes to the other has declined. This evolution is consistent with the observed decline in multihoming and has important implications for competition and the long-run structure of the consumer AI market. In sum, our demand estimates point to three sources of competitive pressure: limited horizontal differentiation, strong substitution in response to quality improvements, and the declining incremental value of additional subscriptions. Under differentiatedproducts Bertrand–Nash pricing, these forces put downward pressure on equilibrium markups. We then use our demand estimates to calibrate the supply side of the model. We estimate markups, expressed as a share of the price (i.e., Lerner Index) ranging from 19% to 59% across products, suggesting that about 41-81% of revenues are used to cover the marginal costs of running these AI models. In our dynamic extension with endogenous improvements in model quality , we find even lower markups. In particular, when providers internalize the future value of expanding their user bases, the marginal cost of operating a typical service is roughly 70% to 80% of its subscription price. These estimates capture the variable marginal costs of providing AI services but exclude fixed operating costs and expenditures on research and model development. Thus, they are an upper bound on total profitability . The model also allows us to conduct counterfactual analyses and quantify the consumer surplus generated by paid AI services. We estimate that access to paid AI subscriptions generates average consumer surplus of approximately $1.09 per consumer per quarter. This average masks substantial heterogeneity because most consumers do not currently subscribe to an AI service. Among adopters, paid AI services generate average consumer surplus of approximately $35 each quarter, over and above the amount spent on AI subscriptions. We also use the model to examine how consumer preferences for AI services shape competition. We begin by considering substitutability across services. By the end of our sample, all pairs of AI services are substitutes on average: the marginal utility of an additional subscription is lower for a consumer who already subscribes to another service. For some services, such as Anthropic which is very substitutable with OpenAI, equilibrium prices would be 30% higher under a counterfactual with no substitutability , and up to 60% higher if the services were complements, as several service pairs were early in our sample. The strong correlation in consumers’ preferences across providers also constrains markups by limiting product differentiation. In a counterfactual in which preferences across providers are uncorrelated, and services are therefore more differentiated, equilibrium prices are approximately 2% to 10% higher. Finally , we examine Anthropic’s effect on competition. Although OpenAI remains the dominant provider, Anthropic has grown rapidly from a small base since the release of Claude Code. To quantify Anthropic’s competitive role, we consider a counterfactual in which Anthropic is removed from the market. Because consumers’ preferences for the two providers’ services are highly correlated and the services are strong substitutes, Anthropic exerts meaningful competitive discipline on OpenAI. In the counterfactual, OpenAI would raise its prices modestly , but sufficiently that its equilibrium market share would fall relative to its market share in the baseline scenario when it competes with Anthropic. The joint price and adoption response is consistent with Anthropic constraining OpenAI’s exercise of market power. Accounting for the fact that other providers change prices in response to entry amplifies the welfare gain of having Anthropic in the market by 21%, to $5.05 per quarter per AI user. Taken together, our results provide new evidence on consumer demand for generative AI services. Despite AI’s prominence in public discourse, paid consumer adoption remains modest, although recent trends suggest that it will continue to grow rapidly . The limited persistence of paid subscriptions, correlation in preferences, and the shift from complementarity toward substitutability have important implications for the diffusion of AI services and the industry’s long-run competitive structure. Related Literature Our paper contributes to a rapidly growing literature on the adoption and use of generative AI. Recent evidence suggests that exposure to generative AI is now common among both consumers and workers. Survey estimates (e.g., Bicket al., 2026a; Gottfriedet al., 2026a) show that around half of U.S. adults have used generative AI, and that around a quarter to half of U.S. employees have used generative AI for work (e.g., Bicket al., 2026c; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 2026; Kemp, 2025; Bicket al., 2026b). AI adoption for business tasks is also growing inside the firm (Bonneyet al., 2026), and at the executive level (Yotzovet al., 2026). Our analysis complements these survey-based studies by using transaction-level panel data to identify payments to specific AI providers and follow the same consumers over time. This allows us to study provider-specific adoption, multihoming, switching, and retention, and their implications for competition. Our measure is also deliberately narrower than survey-based measures which capture free and enterprise use. Others use non-survey data to study AI adoption. Among these, descriptive industry reports (Bank of America Institute, 2026; PNC Economics Research, 2026) are the closest to our use of transaction-level data. Using aggregated Bank of America data, Bank of America Institute (2026) reports that roughly 3% of households pay for AI services and that paid adoption is concentrated among younger and higher-income households, consistent with our first descrip- tive findings. Demireret al.(2025) use API usage data from OpenRouter and Microsoft Azure (platforms primarily serving developers and technology firms) to document rapid entry , falling prices, and frequent turnover among leading LLMs. We find similar evidence of substantial competitive pressure in the consumer AI market. Caoui (2026) uses data from LMArena, where users choose between anonymized LLM responses, to study preferences over model capabilities and response styles. Data from AI providers have also been used to analyze how consumers use AI products: for example, Chatterjiet al.(2025) and Handaet al.(2025) find that writing, information, and software development are particularly common use cases. Second, we contribute to emerging work quantifying the impacts and value of generative AI. Most closely related is Brynjolfssonet al.(2026) who use online choice experiments to elicit the compensation consumers would require to give up access to generative AI chatbot tools for one month. In March 2026, they estimate a mean willingness to accept of $124.50 per month and a median willingness to accept of $11.40. Their welfare object is complementary , but different from ours. Their estimates capture the value of access to generative AI tools, including services available without a paid subscription, whereas we estimate the incremental surplus generated by paid products relative to an outside option that may include free or employer-provided access. More broadly , we relate to a number of recent works that study the effects of AI tools on economic outcomes such as productivity and firm performance (e.g., Noy and Zhang, 2023; Chen and Chan, 2024; Cuiet al., 2024; Chen and Stratton, 2026; Otiset al., 2024; Dillonet al., 2025; Songet al., 2026; Sarkar, 2025; Brynjolfssonet al., 2025; Hampoleet al., 2025; Babina et al., 2026), as well as the impact of consumers delegating purchase choices (e.g., Delaprez and Hortaçsu, 2026) and financial decision-making (e.g., Choukhmaneet al., 2026; Luet al., 2025). Building on this literature, we study the welfare implications of AI market structure, complementing existing work on the potential welfare impact of increased productivity , worker displacement, or changes in economic behavior (e.g., Athey and Morton, 2025). Finally , our paper relates to the industrial organization literature on demand estimation, new products, and consumer welfare (Berryet al., 1995, 2004; Nevo, 2000). Petrin (2002) demonstrates how demand-estimation methods and consumer-level information can be used to quantify the welfare gains generated by a new product, focusing on the introduction of the minivan. Our model is most closely related to Gentzkow (2007), who develops a demand model that allows for both heterogeneity in consumer preferences and complementarity across products to value online newspapers, and the broader demand estimation literature that allows for complementarity between products (Hendel, 1999; Dubé, 2004; Thomassenet al., 2017; Allen and Rehbeck, 2019; Compiani, 2022; Iaria and Wang, 2020; Wang, 2024; Ershovet al., 2025). We adapt the framework from Gentzkow (2007) to the rapidly evolving market for subscription AI services and use panel data to separately identify persistent preference heterogeneity and complementarities across providers. We extend the framework by allowing both to evolve over time, and connect the demand estimates to equilibrium price competition. These features allow us to quantify the surplus generated by paid AI services and study how changing relationships among providers affect competition and the industry’s long-run structure. 2 Data Our main data is a panel of anonymized credit and debit card transactions from Fiserv, a leading provider of payments and financial services technology solutions. Our sample covers January 2021 through April 2026 and includes information on 114 billion transactions from 719 million cards and 174 million consumers. To limit our sample to instances in which we likely observe individuals’ primary cards, our baseline sample restricts to individual-months with at least 20 transactions. This restriction reduces our sample to 82 million consumers. The transaction-level data allow us to study within-consumer purchasing patterns over time and across products. This, in turn, enables us to provide novel evidence on competition and substitution among AI products. For each transaction, we observe the purchase date and amount; anonymized card and cardholder identifiers; and the merchant’s name, industry , and location. The data also include consumer demographics, such as age, income group, and ZIP code. Table 1 reports summary statistics for our sample of consumers. In January 2026, consumers in our sample made an average of 63 transactions and spent an average of $3,268 over the month. The sample spans the income distribution: 15% of consumers have annual incomes below $50,000, while 16% have incomes above $200,000. It also covers all age groups, with 46% of consumers aged 55 or older and 9% aged 34 or younger. We identify AI-related transactions primarily using merchant names (Appendix A.1 includes additional details). We focus on the four large generative AI providers observed in our data: Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), OpenAI (ChatGPT), and xAI (Grok). Our analysis is restricted to paid consumer accounts, which capture realized consumer demand and provide revealed-preference evidence of consumers’ willingness to pay . They also measure a key source of revenue for providers. Our data do not capture free consumer accounts or enterprise accounts. For some analyses, we also identify transactions for a number of other subscription products, including Grammarly , Chegg, Netflix, Spotify , and the New York Times. Other Data Sources.We obtain model-capability measures from the Epoch AI Capabilities Index, which assesses performance across a broad range of tasks (Epoch AI, 2025). Figure 1a plots the index for each provider’s frontier model over time. Model capabilities vary substantially over time but relatively little across providers at a given date, showing that AI providers’ frontier models have thus far advanced at similar rates. We collect product prices from company announcements and archived webpages. We focus on each company’s core entry-level product, which is priced between $19.99 and $30 per month for each provider throughout our sample. Figure 1b shows that, across all providers, the vast majority of those who pay for a product in our data pay less than $35 per month, consistent with the dominance of these entry-level products. 3 Motivating Evidence: AI Adoption, Multihoming, and Churn To begin examining the competitive dynamics of the consumer AI industry , we document several new facts about paid AI adoption. We find that multihoming is common but has declined over time, that churn is high relative to other subscription products, and that consumers are particularly likely to move across providers around model releases. These facts motivate and discipline the model developed in Section 4. 3.1 Patterns of AI Adoption Overall Trends.Consumer use of paid AI products has grown over time, although adoption has varied across providers. Figure 1c shows that by April 2026, 2.9% of consumers paid for at least one of the four major AI products in our sample. Scaling by the number of U.S. credit card holders implies that over 6 million individuals paid for a consumer AI service that month— roughly equal to the combined subscriber bases of the Wall Street Journal and The Economist, or about two-thirds the size of YouTube TV’s subscriber base. OpenAI accounted for the largest share, with 2.4% of all consumers subscribing. Anthropic, however, experienced particularly rapid growth following the release of Claude 4.6 in February 2026: the share of purchasers tripled from January 2026 to April 2026. Adoption is highest along the coasts and in major metropolitan areas: California, Washington, Florida, and the Mid-Atlantic exhibit particularly high rates of AI adoption. By contrast, adoption is much lower in less densely populated areas in the South and Midwest. Appendix Figures C.1 and C.2 show more localized adoption patterns within Massachusetts and New York City . Panels (a) and (b) of Figure 3 show that adoption is higher among highincome and younger consumers. As of April 2026, consumers earning over $200,000 annually are 1.7 times as likely to adopt as those earning less than $50,000. Many consumers pay for more than one AI product in a given month, though multihoming has declined over time. These patterns help identify substitutability over time in the model. Multihoming at OpenAI and Anthropic.To begin, Figure 4a focuses on the two most popular providers as of April 2026, OpenAI and Anthropic. The extent to which AI products act as substitutes, rather than complements, affects both demand and pricing, as we explore in our model. 3.3 Churn is High and Switching Across Providers is Common We next look at patterns of churn and substitution across providers. However, their spending in other categories does not appear to strongly differ from that of matched non-adopters. 4 Model Motivated by our empirical evidence, in this section, we develop a structural model of demand for paid AI services. The model allows us to characterize consumer preferences, their change over time, and implications for market competition. We then use the model to study the equilibrium structure of the consumer AI market and implications of competition on welfare. 4.1 Setup We model consumers’ decisions about which AI services to use as a discrete choice problem in which consumers may choose bundles of services rather than a single service. Our results in Section 3.2 show that consumers frequently multihome across providers. Following Gentzkow (2007), our model distinguishes between two explanations for this multihoming. First, services may be complements, so that combinations of providers are more valuable than the sum of their individual components. Second, multihoming may reflect correlated preference heterogeneity , whereby consumers who strongly prefer one provider also tend to prefer others. Each consumerichooses a bundle of AI services from the set of servicesJ= 1, . . . , J. For tractability , we restrict consumers to choosing at most two services. The choice setCtherefore consists of the outside option, theJindividual services, and the �J  two-service bundles. We let c∈ Cdenote a bundle and let|c|denote the number of services contained in bundlec. Under our restriction,|c| ∈0,1,2. 4.2 Utility Consumer preferences over AI services are heterogeneous. Consumers differ in their preferences for services throughθ ij, which captures consumeri’s time-invariant taste for servicej. We allow tastes for services offered by different providers to be correlated within a consumer, so that multihoming may arise from correlated preference heterogeneity rather than complementarities between services. We assume that these tastes remain fixed over time. The termsΓ ct andγ ic capture bundle-specific utility that arises when consumers use multiple AI services. In our baseline analysis, we assume providers play a static differentiated-product Bertrand pricing game. We then extend the model to account for dynamic learning by doing incentives. Thus, despite consumers choosing bundles rather than individual services, the equilibrium markup takes the same form as in the standard Bertrand pricing model. The key difference is that the relevant demand elasticity is computed from product demand, which aggregates substitution across all bundles containing servicej. Complementarities enter through the bundle demand system: bundle-specific utility affects the bundle choice probabilities, which in turn determine product demand and its price elasticity . An important implication of the model is that the degree of complementarity between services directly influences firms’ pricing decisions. For example, suppose servicesjandkbecome less complementary (or, equivalently , more substitutable) over time, so thatΓ jkt decreases. Holding all else constant, consumers become less likely to purchase the bundle{j, k}, reducing demand for both services. As a result, providerjfinds it optimal to lower its price. More generally , changes in complementarities affect equilibrium prices through their impact on product demand and its price elasticity . 4.5 Extension: Dynamic Model Quality In our baseline version of the model, firms set prices to compete for consumers, taking product quality as fixed. However, we also consider an extension in which product quality evolves over time and depends, in part, on past adoption. Specifically , we introduce learning by doing, whereby providers improve their products as they accumulate users. This mechanism differs slightly from the traditional learning-by-doing framework, in which accumulated experience lowers the marginal cost of production. In our setting, learning by doing instead improves product quality . This extension allows us to study how competition affects not only current prices and adoption, but also the evolution of future product quality . Consumer Demand.Letω jt denote the quality of providerj’s model at timet. Model quality is one of the observed characteristics contained inX jt and therefore directly affects consumer utility through equation (3). Letβ ω >0denote the marginal utility of model quality . Thus, all else equal, improvements in model quality increase current demand. Because current demand determines the number of users from whom a provider learns, higher quality today can increase adoption, which in turn improves future product quality and future demand. Evolution of Product Quality.We assume that model quality evolves according to ωjt =ρ 0 +ρω j,t−1 +λs j,t−1 +ϕ t +η jt,(13) wheres j,t−1 denotes the share of consumers using providerjin periodt−1. The parameterρ captures persistence in product quality , whileλgoverns the extent of learning by doing. When λ >0, a larger user base today improves the provider’s product quality in the following period. The termϕ t captures changes in the state of AI technology that are common across providers, whileη jt is an idiosyncratic model-quality productivity shock. Dynamic Pricing.Because current demand affects future product quality , the link between adoption and learning makes the provider’s pricing problem dynamic. Given current model qualitiesω t, providers choose prices to maximize the present discounted value of profits. Let Vj(ωt)denote providerj’s value function. Providerjsolves Vj(ωt) = maxpjt {sjt(pjt −κ jt) +ϱE t [Vj(ωt+1)]},(14) whereϱ∈(0,1)denotes the provider’s discount factor. In particular, a lower price for providerjincreases its own current demand and therefore its future product quality , while also shifting demand away from competing providers and reducing the experience from which those providers learn. Providers internalize both effects when setting prices. The first-order condition for providerjin the dynamic formulation is: pjt −κ jt = sjt α Z sijt(1−s ijt)dF(θ, γ) −ϱλ JX k=1 Et  ∂Vj(ωt+1) ∂ωk,t+1  ∂skt ∂pjt ∂sjt ∂pjt .(15) The first term on the right-hand side corresponds to the standard static markup in equation (12). The second term captures the dynamic value of changing the allocation of users across providers through its effect on future model quality . A change in providerj’s price affects not only its own user base and future quality , but also the user bases and future qualities of competing providers. The magnitude of this dynamic incentive depends on the strength of learning by doing,λ, and on how changes in each provider’s future quality affect providerj’s continuation value. The own-quality component of the dynamic term gives providers an incentive to lower current prices in order to attract users and improve their future products. At the same time, a lower price can reduce competitors’ future quality by shifting users away from them, providing an additional strategic incentive to compete for users today . When there is no learning by doing (λ= 0), these dynamic incentives disappear and the pricing condition collapses to the static pricing condition in equation (12). 5 Estimation We estimate the demand model in two steps. First, we recover consumer preferences via maximum likelihood using panel data on consumer adoption patterns. The estimation identifies the joint distribution of consumer preferences over product characteristics. The panel structure—using repeated observations for a given consumer over time—is valuable for identifying persistent consumer heterogeneity , while substitution patterns over time identify the correlation in unobserved tastes across products and substitutability of products. Second, we relate the estimated preference parameters to observable product characteristics, such as price and model quality , to quantify the sources of consumer heterogeneity . We then calibrate the supply side of the model. Combining the demand-side estimates with the providers’ first-order conditions allows us to recover each provider’s marginal cost parameters. Later, we will conduct counterfactuals with our demand-side estimates to study implications of competition on prices and welfare. 5.1 Distribution of Heterogeneous Preferences Consumers’ preferences in equation (2) include a common time- and service-varying component,δ jt; a heterogeneous individual- and service-specific component,θ ij; a common time- and bundle-varying component,Γ ct; and a heterogeneous individual- and bundle-specific component,γ ic. Here, we describe how we parameterize the heterogeneity in consumers’ preferences, θij andγ ic. We allow consumers’ preferences and the degree of complementarity and substitutability across AI services to be heterogeneous and correlated. We assume that consumers’ persistent preference heterogeneity ,(θi,γ i), follows a multivariate normal distribution: θi i.i.d.∼ N(0,Σ θ),γ i i.i.d.∼ N(0,Σ γ),(16) The vectorθ i captures heterogeneous preferences for individual AI services, whileγ i captures heterogeneous preferences for service bundles. We allow preferences for individual services to be correlated within a consumer, so the covariance matrixΣθ is unrestricted. For tractability , we assume that preferences for service bundles are independent across bundles and independent of service-specific preferences: Σγ = diag � σ2γ,cc∈C2 ,Cov �θi,γ i =0.(17) Allowing for both persistent preference heterogeneity and bundle-specific utility flows enables the model to distinguish between two explanations for the multihoming observed in the data. Consumers may adopt multiple AI services because the services are complements—for example, because ChatGPT increases the value of Claude—or because consumers with strong preferences for one service also tend to have strong preferences for the other. The first mechanism is captured by the bundle-specific preference terms, while the second is captured by correlation in consumers’ service-specific preferences. 5.2 Demand Estimation Maximum Likelihood Estimation.We estimate the model by maximum likelihood using our quarterly panel of individual bundle choices over the period 2024Q1-2026Q1. The mean utility terms,δ jt andΓ ct, are identified primarily from average choice frequencies. For example, if ChatGPT has a large market share, this implies a high value ofδ ChatGPT,t. Similarly , if the ChatGPT–Claude bundle is chosen more frequently than would be predicted based on the individual market shares of ChatGPT and Claude, this suggests a higher value of Γct, all else equal. The distribution of preference heterogeneity ,(Σ θ,Σ γ), is identified from persistent withinconsumer choice behavior. For example, if a consumer repeatedly chooses ChatGPT over time, this persistence cannot be fully explained byδ jt becauseδ jt is common across consumers. Instead, such behavior is indicative of persistent heterogeneity in preferences. More generally , the diagonal elements ofΣ θ andΣ γ are identified from the extent to which consumers repeatedly make similar choices over time. The off-diagonal elements ofΣ θ are identified from co-adoption and substitution patterns across AI services. For example, if consumers who currently use or previously used Claude are systematically more likely to adopt ChatGPT, this implies a positive covariance between preferences for the two services, i.e., Cov(θi,ChatGPT, θi,Claude)>0.(22) Empirically , a central challenge is separating the interaction terms,Γct, from correlated preference heterogeneity ,(Σθ,Σ γ). For example, frequent selection of the ChatGPT-Claude bundle could indicate that the products are complements, but could also reflect persistent unobserved heterogeneity: some consumers may simply have high demand for AI products. We distinguish these channels using panel variation, following the logic of Gentzkow (2007). The key identifying assumption is that the correlated component of unobserved preferences is persistent over time. Under this assumption, if two AI products are complements, a consumer should be more likely to use both products in the same periods and neither in others. By contrast, if multi-homing is driven by correlated taste heterogeneity , high-AI-type consumers will have persistently high demand for AI tools, but may switch between single-homing and multi-homing as relative product quality changes, including around model releases, as suggested by Figure 6. 6In December 2024, xAI raised prices of Premium+ from $16 to $22. In February 2025, after the release of Grok 3, they introduced SuperGrok at $30 and raised the price of Premium+ to $40 (see, e.g., Mehta, 2025). 5.3 Supply Calibration Using the estimated parameters, observed market shares and prices, and the providers’ firstorder conditions (eq. 12), we calibrate the supply side of the model, which consists of the providers’ marginal costs of providing AI services,κ jt. Rearranging eq. (12), we solve for marginal costs as κjt =p jt − sjt ˆα Z sijt(1−s ijt)d ˆF(θ, γ) .(23) We directly observe prices and market shares in the data. The remaining terms depend on the model estimates: we compute the individual choice probabilitiess ijt at the estimated parameters and approximate the integral by simulation, drawing from ˆF(θ, γ). 6 Results Our model results suggest that paid consumer demand for AI is sensitive to quality and prices, that our multihoming patterns in Section 3 are driven by correlated preferences rather than complementarities in the products themselves, and that AI products are becoming more substitutable over time. Substantial preference heterogeneity implies that the welfare effects of AI are concentrated among heavy AI users. 6.1 Consumer Preferences We report our estimates of consumer preferences in Table 3. Throughout, we convert utility estimates into willingness-to-pay by dividing by the estimated price coefficientˆα. Panel (a) displays our mean preference parameters. Consistent with the overall market shares, the results suggest that the typical consumer prefers OpenAI products relative to other alternatives, a preference that has remained stable over time. For example, our estimates imply that the average consumer was willing to pay a $10 premium per month for OpenAI products relative to Anthropic products at the end of the sample in 2026Q1. The bottom row of panel (a) displays the standard deviations of preference heterogeneity . The results indicate that there is substantial heterogeneity in how individuals value AI, which is unsurprising given the variation in adoption patterns. The standard deviations range from 5.5 to 6 across providers, which is substantial relative to the mean valuations (on average 34% of the size). Consumers in the top quartile of the preference distribution for ChatGPT are willing to pay $37 more per month for ChatGPT than consumers in the bottom quartile. In addition to heterogeneity , our estimates suggest that consumers are relatively sensitive to prices and model quality . The first row of panel (b) displays our estimates of consumers’ price sensitivity and how they value AI capabilities. In each specification, we estimate a negative and significant monthly price coefficient. Our instrumental variables estimate is -0.22 which implies an average price elasticity of -4.6; that is a 10% increase in price lowers demand by 46%. The second row of panel (b) displays the quality coefficient, which suggests that moving from ChatGPT’s Model 4 in March 2023 to Model 5.5 in April 2026 increased the value to consumers by $25 per month. In other words, consumers are indifferent between GPT-4 and paying a $25 per month premium to access Model GPT-5.5. Panel (c) displays the correlations in preference heterogeneity . The results suggest that a consumer’s preferences for AI are positively correlated within an individual. The correlation in preferences between ChatGPT and Claude is 0.89. Customers who value xAI and Google tend to have lower preferences for the other AI providers, consistent with both serving a distinct consumer segment from general-purpose AI assistants. (Gemini, for example, is often bundled with GoogleOne products). As a result, the high levels of multihoming seen in Figure 4 are likely due to correlated preferences rather than complementarities. Indeed, panel (d) displays the mean and standard deviation of the complementarity between different AI providers over time. The results suggest that products like OpenAI and Google were complements at the beginning of the sample, but have since become substitutes. OpenAI and Anthropic were always substitutes, even more so towards the end of the sample. Holding preferences fixed at their values at the start of the sample, so that the comparison isolates the complementarity channel from correlated tastes, the probability that users with Claude would also have ChatGPT decreased by 83% over the sample. This decline in complementarity increases competition: it reduces demand for each service and, all else equal, puts downward pressure on equilibrium prices, as will be illustrated in Section 7. 6.2 Welfare Our estimated model implies that the welfare effects of AI are heterogeneous across consumers, and have increased over time as models have improved. Consistent with the substantial preference heterogeneity we estimate in Table 3 panel (a), the surplus from AI is highly concentrated: consumers in the top decile of the OpenAI taste distribution capture over 97% of consumer surplus. As AI models improved over the two years in our sample, total consumer surplus has increased over five-fold. Since the utility shocks,ν ict, in equation 2 are distributed Type-I Extreme Value, the expected indirect utility from access to choice setC t in dollars is: Wit(Ct) = 1α log X c∈Ct exp(uict) +K ! .(24) whereu ict = Pj∈c(δjt +θ ij) + Γct +γ ic is the deterministic component of consumeri’s utility from choosing bundlecin periodtandKis the Euler-Mascheroni constant. Therefore the change in consumer surplus is: ∆CS Oit = 1α  log X c∈Ct exp(uict) ! −log   X c∈C−Ot exp(uict)     .(25) Results.Figure 7 plots total consumer welfare from paid AI products. The welfare gain from AI has risen five-fold in the two years prior to 2026Q1, from $0.20 per quarter to over $1.09 per quarter. Since OpenAI has the largest market share among paid consumers, 74% of the welfare gain from consumer AI products can be attributed to OpenAI. Recent growth in Anthropic implies that by 2026Q1, welfare from Anthropic has risen to $0.13 per quarter. The average increase in welfare masks substantial heterogeneity because most consumers do not currently subscribe to an AI service. Dividing each average welfare gain by the share of consumers paying for any AI service, the normalized quarterly gains are $35 for all AI products in 2026Q1, with $26 attributable to OpenAI and $4 attributable to Anthropic. 6.3 Supply Parameters Table 4 shows our estimates of markups, estimated with and without dynamic model quality . With a static supply-side (Equation 23), the model implies that OpenAI charges a markup of approximately $12 per month (Lerner index of 59%), whereas Anthropic charges a markup of $9 per month. Anthropic charges a lower markup, in part, because OpenAI and Anthropic are substitutes. Our model with dynamic quality incentives suggests an even more competitive market than in the baseline model. Full details on our dynamic calibration are in Section B.2. With dynamic model quality , Column 2 shows that implied markups are lower for all providers, but significantly so for OpenAI, falling from an implied markup of $12 per month to $4 per month. This is because OpenAI has the largest customer base, so if the dynamic quality incentive is meaningful, it would be strongest for OpenAI. Overall, our dynamic model estimates suggest that marginal costs account for roughly 70-80% of revenues. Our estimates are an upper bound on profitability as they ignore fixed operating costs and research and development expenditures. 7 Counterfactuals and Implications for Competition We use our model to examine how product substitutability and preference heterogeneity shape competition. We find that equilibrium prices would be substantially higher if AI products were, on average, complements rather than substitutes or if consumers’ preferences across products were independent rather than positively correlated. Because Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s products are particularly close substitutes and consumers’ preferences for them are highly correlated, Anthropic plays an important role in constraining market power despite its relatively small current market share. A counterfactual without Anthropic indicates that a meaningful share of the resulting welfare loss comes from higher prices charged by the remaining providers (in addition to the direct loss of access to Anthropic’s products). 7.1 Effects of Substitutability on Competition The increased substitutability between AI products has several important implications for market structure. As in Gentzkow (2007), even though multihoming rates are unconditionally high, our model suggests that this is largely from correlated preference heterogeneity rather than AI products exhibiting strong complementarities. To illustrate the impact of substitutability on prices and market shares, we consider a counterfactual in 2026Q1 whereΓ counter = 0and Γcounter =|Γ|. Without substitutability , consumers respond by being more likely to bundle AI products together. This increases the share of consumers using AI, but providers dampen this effect by raising prices since there is more market power. Table 5 shows that ifΓ = 0, prices would be higher for all providers, and in net, shares of most providers would be higher than the baseline (Figure 8 plots counterfactual shares over time). Anthropic is a particularly interesting case. In this counterfactual, Anthropic raises their prices from $20 per month to $26 per month. However, even with this price change, Anthropic’s market share nearly doubles, from 0.50% to 0.96%. OpenAI, GoogleAI and xAI experience smaller changes in prices and shares. The disproportionate increase in Anthropic’s market shares and prices are likely because OpenAI (which has the largest baseline market share) is by far the most substitutable with Anthropic:Γ OpenAI, Anthropic = -6.44, compared with ΓOpenAI, Google = -0.90 andΓ OpenAI, xAI = -0.04. Our results are stronger if AI products were all complements rather than neither complements nor substitutes. Relative to the baseline, we find that with|Γ|, providers increase their prices by $6-$12 per month. The share of consumers paying for OpenAI and Anthropic rises to 3.02% and 2.33%, respectively , representing a percentage increase of 16% and 364%. Overall, these results suggest that as AI providers have evolved into general-purpose technologies, their products have become increasingly substitutable. As a result, the marketplace has become more competitive, putting downward pressure on prices. 7.2 Impact of Correlated Preferences on Competition Product differentiation is an important source of market power. Although we find substantial heterogeneity in consumers’ overall preferences for AI, there is limited differentiation in their preferences across providers. As shown in panel (c) of Table 3, preferences for AI products are highly correlated. Conditional on how much a consumer likes AI overall, the consumer tends to have similarly favorable preferences for all AI providers. To illustrate the importance of correlated preferences for competition, Table 5 considers a counterfactual in which preferences are uncorrelated, so the off-diagonal entries ofΣθ are zero. Under this counterfactual, prices would be unambiguously higher in 2026Q1. In particular, all providers modestly increase their prices, with changes ranging from 2.1% for OpenAI, which has the smallest price response, to 8.7% for xAI, which has the largest price response. The directional change in market shares differs across providers. The market shares of Anthropic and xAI increase by 28.8% and 29.8%, respectively , whereas the market shares of OpenAI and GoogleAI decrease slightly—by less than 3%. Intuitively , Anthropic’s preferences are the most strongly correlated with those of the other three providers. Its market share therefore increases substantially when consumers who prefer Anthropic no longer have strong preferences for its competitors. xAI also experiences a sizable increase in market share because preferences for xAI and GoogleAI are highly correlated in the baseline and GoogleAI is cheaper. As a result, GoogleAI exerts substantial competitive pressure on xAI in the baseline, which is removed in the counterfactual. 7.3 Welfare Effects of Entry Our estimates imply that AI products are close substitutes, creating competitive pressure among providers. A central implication is that the presence of an individual provider—even one that is not the market leader—may meaningfully constrain the prices charged by its rivals. To quantify this competitive discipline, we consider a counterfactual in which Anthropic is removed from the market in 2026Q1 and allow the remaining providers to reoptimize their prices. Anthropic is a particularly informative case because it is a close substitute for OpenAI, while its users also have overlapping preferences for xAI and GoogleAI. The counterfactual therefore illustrates how the loss of one provider propagates through equilibrium prices, market shares, and consumer welfare. Panel (a) of Figure 9 shows the effect of Anthropic’s counterfactual exit on equilibrium prices. OpenAI and xAI increase their prices by 2.0% and 1.1%, respectively , whereas GoogleAI changes its price by -4.4%. Thus, removing Anthropic does not uniformly increase the market power of every remaining provider. Instead, its effects depend on the patterns of substitution and preference correlation across products. Although the price responses are modest in magnitude, they are notable given Anthropic’s small market share. As we show below, these price changes also affect paid adoption and contribute meaningfully to the change in consumer surplus. Panel (b) shows that the changes in equilibrium market shares are similarly heterogeneous. Interestingly , OpenAI’s market share changes by -0.7%, even though its closest substitute has been removed from the market. This seemingly counterintuitive result reflects OpenAI’s en- dogenous pricing response. Anthropic’s removal relaxes the competitive constraint on OpenAI, allowing it to raise its price. This price increase more than offsets the direct inflow of consumers who would otherwise switch from Anthropic to OpenAI, causing OpenAI’s equilibrium market share to fall. GoogleAI’s market share also falls, by -7.0%, whereas xAI’s market share increases by 17.1%. xAI’s disproportionate response reflects the distribution of consumers’ preferences for bundling. Although OpenAI and Anthropic are the most substitutable pair on average, as captured byΓ, the individual-level estimates ofΓfor xAI and Anthropic have very low dispersion. Consequently , most Anthropic users view xAI as a net substitute, and removing Anthropic shifts many of these users toward xAI despite xAI’s higher equilibrium price. GoogleAI and Anthropic, by contrast, are not strong net substitutes. Moreover, xAI’s expansion intensifies competition with GoogleAI because preferences for these two products are highly correlated, reducing GoogleAI’s market power and inducing it to lower its price. Accounting for these supply-side responses is important for evaluating welfare. The direct loss of access to Anthropic understates the total welfare effect because the remaining providers endogenously adjust their prices. In particular, the price increases by OpenAI and xAI amplify the direct welfare loss from removing Anthropic. Panel (c) shows that, when expressed per AI user, removing Anthropic reduces welfare by $5.05 per quarter. This general-equilibrium welfare loss is 21% larger than the partial-equilibrium loss reported in Section 6.2. Overall, the counterfactual demonstrates that competition in the AI market depends not only on the number and market shares of providers, but also on the structure of substitution among their products. Because consumer preferences are highly correlated across providers and AI products are strong substitutes, Anthropic impacts its rivals’ prices even though consumers frequently use multiple products. Removing Anthropic therefore generates welfare losses beyond the direct loss of access to its product, as the pricing responses of the remaining providers amplify the initial harm. 8 Conclusion We document new patterns in consumer demand for paid generative AI services. Despite AI’s prominence in public and business discourse, paid consumer adoption remains relatively modest, although it grew rapidly toward the end of our sample. In April 2026, 2.4% of consumers paid for an OpenAI product, making OpenAI the most widely adopted provider. Paid adoption of Anthropic products also increased substantially during the final months of our sample. Adoption is concentrated among younger and higher-income consumers. We also find that paid demand exhibits limited persistence and that multihoming across providers is common, particularly early in the sample, although multihoming has declined over time. Our structural model provides additional insight into these patterns. We estimate substan- tial heterogeneity in consumer preferences, but that preferences for general-purpose AI services are highly correlated across providers. At the same time, the relationship between OpenAI and Anthropic has evolved: the two services have become increasingly substitutable over time. This shift is consistent with the growing overlap in their capabilities. Our supply-side model shows how these demand patterns shape competition. Increasing substitutability and overlap among services intensify price competition. In particular, consumers view services from Anthropic and OpenAI as close substitutes. These competitive forces affect both the total welfare generated by paid AI services and the division of surplus between consumers and providers. The resulting limits on firms’ ability to sustain market power also bear directly on firm valuations throughout the industry . 28

chunks.title: Climate Change Impacts on Energy Systems
chunks.text: Climate change impacts on the energy system: a review of trends and gaps Jennifer Cronin1 & Gabrial Anandarajah1 & Olivier Dessens1 Received: 16 August 2017 / Accepted: 20 July 2018 / Published online: 6 August 2018 # The Author(s) 2018 Abstract Major transformation of the global energy system is required for climate change mitigation. However, energy demand patterns and supply systems are themselves subject to climate change impacts. These impacts will variously help and hinder mitigation and adaptation efforts, so it is vital they are well understo od and incorporated into models used to study energy system decarbonisation pathways. To assess the current state of understanding of this topic and identify research priorities, this paper critically reviews the literature on the impacts of climate change on the energy supply system, summarising the regional coverage of studies, trends in their results and sources of disagreement. We then examine the ways in which these impacts have been represented in integrated assessment models of the electricity or energy system. Studies tend to agree broadly on impacts for wind, solar and thermal power stations. Projections for impacts on hydropower and bioenergy resources are more varied. Key uncertainties and gaps remain due to the variation between climate projections, modelling limitations and the regional bias of research interests. Priorities for future research include the following: further regional impact studies for developing countries; studies examining impacts of the changing variability of renewable resources, extreme weather events and combined hazards; inclusion of multiple climate feedback mechanisms in IAMs, accounting for adaptation options and climate model uncertainty. 1 Introduction Major decarbonisation of the energy system has a large part to play in climate change mitigation (Bruckner et al.2014). However, components of the energy system are also affected by climate change itself, via long-term changes in

weather events (Field et al. 2014). In this fast-moving field of research, it is vital that we take stock of the literature quantifying the impacts, assess how that understanding is being used in energy system models and identify key research priorities. Climate change impacts are expected throughout the energy system. On the demand side, the balance of heating and cooling demand patterns is changing due to rising temperatures. On the supply side, impacts include changes t o the averages and variability of wind, solar and hydropower resources; the availability of crops for bioenergy feedstocks; costs and availability of fossil fuels due to melting sea ice and permafrost; the efficiency of PV panels, thermo-electric power plants and transmission lines due to rising temperatures; technology downtime due to changes in the frequency and in tensity of extreme weather events (Ebinger and V ergara2011). These physical effects have implications for the reliability, cost and local environmental impacts of energy supply. Furthermore, some impacts may result in an increased use of fossil fuels or reinforced infrastructure, and thereby increase greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions; for example, reductions in the efficiency of power stations, reductions in renewable energy resources or increased risks of storm damage to coastal infrastructure. These would undermine efforts to decarbonise the energy sector. To ensure mitigation and adaptation

chunks.title: Climate Change Impacts on Energy Systems
chunks.text: ductions in renewable energy resources or increased risks of storm damage to coastal infrastructure. These would undermine efforts to decarbonise the energy sector. To ensure mitigation and adaptation options can be comprehensively examined, it is therefore imperative that climate change impacts are thoroughly accounted for in the models which are used to examine the feasibility, costs and implications of energy system decarbonisation pathways. Further research into climate impacts on the energy system and their inclusion in cross-sectoral integrated modelling is highlighted in the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5, Clarke et al. 2014). A number of previous reviews examine elements of this topic (Mideksa and Kallbekken 2010; Ebinger and V ergara2011; Schaeffer et al. 2012; Arent et al. 2014; Stanton et al. 2016; Chandramowli and Felder2014; Ciscar and Dowling 2014). These focus largely on the climate change impacts on technologies currently in use and include relatively little discussion of the impacts on technologies which may become important in the future (e.g. bioenergy, carbon capture and storage), the levels of agreement between the results of different studies or the relative importance of impacts within regional energy systems. Comments on the strengths and weaknesses of the models used and the associated confidence that can be assigned to the results are also limited. To facilitate the further inclusion of climate change impacts in integrated assessment models of the electricity or energy system (IAMs), we aim to address these gaps by examining the following research questions: (i) In which areas does the literature largely agree on the direction and magnitude of the impacts? (ii) Which elements are not well covered in the literature? (iii) What are the key reasons for disagreement between results? (iv) How have climate change impacts been incorporated in IAMs? (v) Which research areas should be prioritised?

chunks.title: Climate Change Impacts on Energy Systems
chunks.text:
ered in the literature? (iii) What are the key reasons for disagreement between results? (iv) How have climate change impacts been incorporated in IAMs? (v) Which research areas should be prioritised? This paper provides an updated, extended review of the literature on supply-side climate change impacts. Methods to incorporate impacts on heating and cooling demand in IAMs, mainly with heating and cooling degree days, have already been demonstrated by several IAMs (see OR2). So we focus here on supply-side impacts: on primary resources, generation technologies and energy transport. To examine the robustness of trends indicated in the impacts literature, we examine the levels of agreement between studies and the extent to which the system elements and regions of the world are covered (Section 3). As climate change hazards, physical and operational resilience and adaptation capability vary significantly 80 Climatic Change (2018) 151:79–93

around the world, findings from impacts literature cannot be automatically applied across regions. We discuss the principal sources of disagreement between studies (Section 4) and the ways in which climate impacts have been incorporated into IAMs (Section 5), so that we can finally prioritise the remaining research gaps (Sections 6 and 7). 2 Literature review method For this review, we define ‘impact studies ’ as those which model the physical effects of changing climate on one or more elements of the energy supply system, such as a primary resource or generation technology. We define IAMs as those which represent interactions between the wider electricity or energy system and some part of the earth system such as hydrology or climate. A semi-systematic search method was employed. Supply-side impact studies were identified via the references of previous reviews on this subject (Mideksa and Kallbekken 2010; Ebinger and V ergara 2011; Schaeffer et al. 2012; Chandramowli and Felder 2014) and a SCOPUS search using combinations of

chunks.title: Climate Change Impacts on Energy Systems
chunks.text: e references of previous reviews on this subject (Mideksa and Kallbekken 2010; Ebinger and V ergara 2011; Schaeffer et al. 2012; Chandramowli and Felder 2014) and a SCOPUS search using combinations of keywords relating to climate change, impacts and energy. From those search results, papers were selected providing they were published in English in a peer-reviewed journal since 2000 and focussed explicitly on physical impacts on at least one element of the energy system. For bioenergy, studies referring specifically to dedicated bioenergy crops were included. Studies employing both detailed climate change scenarios and fixed temperature/precipitation inputs were included. A database of the 106 supply-side impact studies, with details of their authors, subjects, modelling techniques and key findings, is presented in the Online Resource 1 (OR1). Studies which have incorporated one or more supply-side climate change impacts in IAMs were identified during the search described above and using additional search terms relating to electricity and integrated models. This method aimed to thoroughly identify the key literature, while remaining flexible and allowing for some judgement on the importance of various elements. 3 Summary of impact studies Table 1 summarises the impacts described in the reviewed studies. Elements of the energy system are affected by changes to average climatic conditions, the variability of conditions and the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events. Impacts studies on wind and hydropower resources dominate the literature, followed by bioenergy resources and the performance of thermo-electric power plants (TPPs). Impacts of gradual changes to climatic parameters such as temperature and precipitation have been studied more than changes to extreme weather events, as existing tools have limited ability to capture extreme events. Wind Reviewing wind impacts literature, Pryor and Barthelmie ( 2010) found average wind speeds around Europe and North America would remain within ± 15% of current values by the end of the century. This limit has since been revised up to ± 20% (Tobin et al.2015;D a v ye ta l . 2017) and ± 30% (Carvalho et al. 2017). Limited studies suggest there will be no significant change in wind resource over China (Chen et al. 2012) or Southern Africa (Fant et al. 2016). Solar Climate change projections tend to agree that cloud cover will decrease in low- to midlatitude regions (Patt et al. 2013); however, increases in solar resource will often be counterbalanced by decreasing efficiency due to rising temperatures. As such, regional studies tend to project changes in solar generation of less than ± 10% by the end of the century (Crook et al. 2011; Gaetani et al. 2014; Panagea et al. 2014). Wave Wave resource is potentially affected by changes to wind patterns and sea level rise. However, limited studies project no change to wave generation in the Persian Gulf (Kamranzad et al. 2015) or Menorca (Sierra et al. 2017) and less than 3% in the UK (Reeve et al. 2011). Bioenergy Both average yields and the areas suitable for growing bioenergy crops are affected by rising temperatures and changing precipitation patterns. Broadly, yields are expected to increase at high latitudes and decrease at low latitudes, for example by as much as − 16% and + 28% in the 2050s (Haberl et al. 2011), though studies note particularly large uncertainties regarding the importance of technological development and CO 2 fertilisation (Haberl et al. 2011; Cosentino et al. 2012). This is expected to shift the suitable land northward for several crops (e.g. various flex food-energy crops in Europe (Tuck et al. 2006), switchgrass in the USA (Barney and DiTomaso 2010) and miscanthus globally (Hager et al. 2014)). Thermal power stations Rising temperatures are expected to reduce power plant output by approximately 0.4–0.7% per degree due to reduced thermal efficiencies (Chuang and Sue 2005;D u r m a y a za n dS o g u t2006;L i n n e r u de ta l .2011; Ibrahim et al. 2014). Reduced water resources for cooling are expected to cause power stations to reduce load or shutdown. For example, an annual mean temperature rise of 3 °C could cause daily reductions of generation capacity of up to 36% in Germany (Koch et al. 2014). While some regions are expected to experience increased capacity under climate change (India and Russia), global annual thermal power plant capacity is likely to be reduced by 7 –12% in the mid-century (van Vliet et al. 2016). present mostly low risks to powerlines in the UK (McColl et al. 2012), but may increase reliability indices by up to 30% in parts of Russia (Tyusov et al. 2017). Certain impacts are less well covered in the literature. Although many papers refer to increasing damage to bioenergy crops and energy infrastructure due to storms (extreme winds, floods, landslides), very few studies were found to quantify these (one for bioenergy, three for infrastructure). No quantitative studies were found on changing maintenance requirements for solar technologies or the availability and costs of fossil fuel resource extraction as sea ice and permafrost melt. As shown in Table 2, the most studied impacts are for hydro and wind power in Europe, followed by North America. Four non-regional studies were identified examining thermodynamic behaviour of nuclear power stations, and the rating and structural failures of overhead lines. Impacts in Australasia, Asia (other than China) and Africa are under-represented. Approximately two thirds of the studies included in this review cover a sub-country, country or multi-country region, while the others are global or plant level. Potential for adaptation to climate change is covered inconsistently. For example, several authors comment that negative impacts on wind and solar generation and infrastructure will be insignificant because rapid development and relatively short lifetimes of these technologies allow adaptation through technological upgrades and siting (e.g. Ebinger and V ergara 2011). Careful siting of new thermal power stations may also be possible to mitigate risk of water shortages. However, most power plants are currently situated where decreasing mean annual streamflow and strongly increasing water temperatures are projected (van

be possible to mitigate risk of water shortages. However, most power plants are currently situated where decreasing mean annual streamflow and strongly increasing water temperatures are projected (van Vliet et al.2016)a n d water competition may be exacerbated in the future by increased deployment of carbon capture and storage and biomass crops (e.g. Chandel et al. 2011; Byers et al. 2016). For siting to be considered a feasible adaptation solution at the local level for any technology, high-resolution national impact studies and communication with industry partners are required. For hydropower, design changes and dam management may also provide adaptation options (Vicuña et al. 2011). van Vliet et al. ( 2016) note that an increase in plant efficiency of approximately 10% would offset the mean annual negative impacts for most regions (greater improvements would be required to offset monthly impacts) but no financial cost is given for this type and level of adaptation. No quantitative studies were found to examine other adaptation options, such as changing water dispatch patterns or regulations on cooling water discharge temperatures, or strengthening generation or transmission infrastructure. As impact studies generally examine one or two elements of the energy system in isolation and there are gaps in the regional coverage of the literature, it is unclear whether the degree to which different impacts have been studied is representative of the impacts ’ perceived importance, or rather the current state of

chunks.text: gional coverage of the literature, it is unclear whether the degree to which different impacts have been studied is representative of the impacts ’ perceived importance, or rather the current state of modelling ability. Relative importance can be assessed most simply by considering the percentage share of generation technologies in different regions, as done for hydropower by Turner et al. (2017). As supply technologies play different roles in the system (e.g. base or peak load generation) and may interact through water use, understanding of the relative importance of impacts and their combined effects m ay be improved by the use of combined modelling approaches (e.g. Rübbelke and Vögele 2013; van Vliet et al. 2016)a n db y the integration of several climate change impacts in models of the wider electricity and energy systems. 4 Sources of disagreement Differences between impact studies appear to be due primarily to two factors: the climate projections used as inputs to the impact models and impact model assumptions. Many studies depend heavily on the modellers ’ choice of GCM(s), especially those for which precipitation is a main driver. For ex ample, various studies note that projections for hydropower and bioenergy resources remain highly uncertain in some regions due to disagreement between GCMs (Hamududu and Killingtveit 2012; De Laporte et al. 2014; Labriet et al. 2015a). As shown in the IPCC AR5 WGI (Stocker et al. 2013), the variation in GCM precipitation results is high over large parts of North and South America, Africa, southern Europe, southern Asia and Australia, especially under the lower emissions scenario. Modelling uncertainty is also important for wind and solar studies. Examining an ensemble of 10 GCMs, Karnauskas et al. ( 2017) conclude that results for some regions (tropics and souther n sub-tropics) are only robust for the later part of the century under the higher emissions scenario. Fant et al. (2016 ) note the high uncertainty in cloud
