We note that adding storage to the system, which we discuss later, reduces curtailment. Net System Costs. In all cases, both capacity value and energy value for VRE are highest for the “more-wind” scenario, suggesting that VRE targets weighted toward higher shares of solar may not be cost optimal. However, levelized costs and economic value of VRE must be taken together to understand the total system cost impacts due to additional VRE capacity. Fig. 4A depicts the net system cost impacts in terms of avoided CO2 emissions. Note that we do not report total system costs but instead cost differences relative to a no-VRE case. This focuses our results on the additional cost of different VRE scenarios. Focusing ﬁrst on the base-case cost scenario, we see that net system costs are well below the US SCC of USD 40 per tCO2, except in the solar-majority scenarios with high VRE penetration. Indeed, the lowest carbon mitigation costs occur for the “balanced” or “more-wind” scenarios, ranging from USD 8 per tCO 2 for 200 GW of VRE to USD 26 per tCO 2 for 600 GW of VRE. The “more-wind” scenarios also have the highest share of VRE generation and avoid the most carbon emissions (SI Appendix, Fig. S12). We note that total carbon emissions for the 600 GW “morewind” mixes are 1,060 million tonnes of CO 2, an amount similar to direct emissions from India’s electricity

chunks.title: Least-Cost Targets for Renewable Energy in India
chunks.text: emissions (SI Appendix, Fig. S12). We note that total carbon emissions for the 600 GW “morewind” mixes are 1,060 million tonnes of CO 2, an amount similar to direct emissions from India’s electricity sector in 2018 (see SI Appendix, Table S1). In other words, pursuing a VRE target of 600 GW with a “more-wind” mix could freeze carbon emissions from India’s electricity sector at the 2018 level. Fig. 4B depicts net system cost impacts per megawatt-hour of load served. This provides insight into the incremental growth in customer tariffs that would be required to recover the added costs of VRE. Focusing again on the base-case cost scenario, we see that solar-majority mixes cost more than “balanced” or “more-wind” scenarios, per megawatt-hour of load served. Concentrating on the “more-wind,” “balanced,” and “more-solar” mixes, we see that these costs lie in range of USD 1 to 2 per MWh of load for 200 GW, USD 5 to 7 per MWh of load for 400 GW, and USD 11 to 13 per MWh of load for 600 GW (Fig. 3), which is 1 to 2%, 7 to 9%, and 14 to 16% of the average cost of supply in India during 2015–2016 (26). We view these base-case costs as upper limits on the system costs of added VRE capacity. Costs of both solar PV and wind are likely to decline with technology improvements and economies of scale (23). These cost trends would make pursuing higher VRE targets increasingly cost effective. For example, in the “low-cost wind and solar” scenario, optimal additional system costs and carbon mitigation costs are negative for the 200 GW target, and 2 to 3 times lower than the base-case cost scenario for the 400 and 600 GW VRE scenario (Fig. 4 A and B). Although we assume all solar capacity is utility scale, we note that distributed solar plants including rooftop PV and urban minigrids have additional beneﬁts such as avoiding land constraints and reduced transmission losses and will likely be part of the solar ﬂeet. However, distributed solar plants have lower capacity factors compared to utility-scale solar and will make solar-majority mixes cost more than “balanced” or “more-wind” scenarios. System Cost Reduction Factors. Our results indicate that system costs and, in particular, the suboptimality of high solar penetration scenarios are

chunks.text: cost more than “balanced” or “more-wind” scenarios. System Cost Reduction Factors. Our results indicate that system costs and, in particular, the suboptimality of high solar penetration scenarios are strongly inﬂuenced by solar curtailment. Curtailment, in turn, stems from low correlation between solar production and demand as well as inﬂexibility of coal plants. We now consider four factors that could plausibly change in the future and would directly impact these drivers of curtailment: coal plant minimum generation levels, energy storage, more urbanized load shapes, and higher coal costs. Lower minimum coal generation levels. We ﬁnd that reducing minimum coal generation levels does not substantially lower system and emissions mitigation costs (Fig. 5 A and SI Appendix , Fig. S11A). Lowering minimum operating levels for coal plants from 70 to 55% (27) increases VRE energy value by reducing curtailment, and, because solar production is curtailed more in the base-case scenarios, this strategy beneﬁts solar-majority mixes more than wind-majority mixes. However, because the impact on total system costs is small, wind-majority or balanced mixes remain the most cost effective for all but the 200-GW VRE scenarios with low-cost solar. Battery storage. Batteries can reduce system costs by reducing VRE curtailment, avoiding expensive energy generation, and avoiding conventional generation capacity but can increase overall costs because of their capital investments and efﬁciency losses incurred in their charge–discharge cycles. The greatest gains due to battery storage in terms of avoided conventional capacity and reduced curtailment accrue to solar-majority mixes (Fig. 5 B and SI Appendix , Fig. S11 B), which is consistent with other studies (17). However, the mix with the lowest carbon mitigation costs changes from “more-wind” or “balanced” to “more-solar” only for the lowest of the VRE targets (200 GW) and when battery costs are low (USD 150 per kWh). For the higher VRE targets of 400 GW to 600 GW, even with low-cost battery storage, the “more-solar” mixes are not the preferred VRE conﬁgurations. At a cost of USD 330 per kWh of battery storage, net system costs of all battery storage scenarios are greater than the base scenario without battery storage, because of both battery investment costs and efﬁciency losses (28, 29). Battery storage becomes increasingly cost effective with greater VRE targets as it captures more value by smoothing the greater variability in VRE generation. But, even at an average low cost of USD 150 per kWh for Deshmukh et al. Least-cost targets and avoided fossil fuel capacity in India’s pursuit of renewable energy PNAS | 5 of 8

battery storage, we ﬁnd that the lowest carbon mitigation cost among all VRE mixes for the 60-GW battery storage is lower than that of the no-storage base scenario only for the highest VRE target of 600 GW. Urbanized future demand. If India were to undergo rapid urbanization and its national demand proﬁle becomes increasingly similar to that of Delhi’s and Mumbai’s, costs of mitigating carbon emissions are likely to be lower than the base scenario (Fig. 5 C and SI Appendix , Fig. S11 C). This is because Delhi’s and Mumbai’s demand proﬁles are better correlated with VRE generation across all mixes and targets, resulting in more new conventional capacity avoided by VRE, and less curtailment, compared to the base-case demand proﬁle. We note, however, that, while these alternate demand futures have the same energy demand as the base scenario, they have higher peak demand, which requires a greater amount of new conventional capacity in all scenarios, including the zero VRE case. If India experiences a lower growth rate of demand ( ∼15% lower than the base case), total carbon emissions are

chunks.title: Least-Cost Targets for Renewable Energy in India
chunks.text: eater amount of new conventional capacity in all scenarios, including the zero VRE case. If India experiences a lower growth rate of demand ( ∼15% lower than the base case), total carbon emissions are lower but costs of mitigating carbon emissions are higher than the base scenario, because of greater VRE curtailment (SI Appendix, section 2 and Fig. S16). Even at this lower demand, new coal and gas capacity is required to meet peak demand, because of the low capacity value of wind and solar (SI Appendix, Fig. S15). Higher coal costs. Higher costs for new coal plants (SI Appendix, Table S3) reﬂecting higher capital costs for environmental compliance equipment to meet India’s stricter environmental norms and higher fuel cost due to rising mining and transportation costs result in small increases in capacity value (≈ USD 1 per MWh of VRE) but signiﬁcant increases in energy value of VRE (25 to 33%) compared to the base scenario (SI Appendix, Fig. S10). As a result, although wind-dominated mixes remain best, net system and emissions mitigation costs decrease across all VRE targets and mixes (Fig. 5D and SI Appendix, Fig. S11D). Conclusions Across most scenarios, including those with different cost and demand trajectories, operational strategies, and battery storage investments, we ﬁnd that a “balanced” or “more-wind” capacity mix for VRE targets will be the cheapest, both for consumers and for mitigating carbon emissions. This result invites revisiting India’s present policies of pursuing a greater share of solar capacity in its VRE targets (100 GW solar in 160 GW of VRE by 2022 and 350 GW solar in 440 GW VRE by 2030). Even in high-VRE scenarios, our model indicates that signiﬁ- cant amounts of coal capacity will be required to support demand growth. Although studies in other regions of the world have found that VRE cannot avoid conventional generation capacity on a one-to-one basis, we ﬁnd that VRE in India has particularly low capacity values and is thus particularly

chunks.title: Least-Cost Targets for Renewable Energy in India
chunks.text: her regions of the world have found that VRE cannot avoid conventional generation capacity on a one-to-one basis, we ﬁnd that VRE in India has particularly low capacity values and is thus particularly ineffective at displacing dispatchable generation capacity requirements. However, these conventional plants will be operated at low plant load factors, which reduces their carbon emissions, but will likely also reduce the cost effectiveness of their operations. A number of factors have the potential to reduce the cost to integrate VRE for the levels we studied. Battery storage holds promise, but only if storage capacity costs fall to the low end of cost forecasts [weighted average cost of ≈ USD 150 per kWh (23)] and if VRE penetration is high (600 GW). VRE cost declines and coal energy cost growth, both of which are likely (23, 30), could, together, result in costs similar to a fossil fuel-dominated system, even with 600 GW of VRE. In sum, our results indicate that a wind-majority portfolio of 600 GW of VRE has the potential to hold India’s 2030 electricity system carbon emissions at 2018 levels, at costs well below the SCC, even in the midst of signiﬁcant growth in demand. A number of options hold promise for further reducing emissions. Some of these are likely to be low in cost, for example, coupling demand response strategies like shifting India’s large agricultural demand to high VRE generation times. Other options such as expanding nuclear and hydropower capacity may hold large potential but may also cost more and have lower public acceptance. All merit further investigation to identify least-cost pathways for India to continue reducing its carbon emissions. Materials and Methods To estimate the levelized costs and economic value of VRE, we developed three models—a spatially explicit VRE site selection and cost model, a capacity investment model, and an economic dispatch model ( SI Appendix, Fig. S1). Although our modeling approach is customized to address the

chunks.title: Least-Cost Targets for Renewable Energy in India
chunks.text: a spatially explicit VRE site selection and cost model, a capacity investment model, and an economic dispatch model ( SI Appendix, Fig. S1). Although our modeling approach is customized to address the speciﬁcs of capacity expansion planning in India, it builds on well-established work. The model has three main decision steps: VRE site selection, conventional generator capacity expansion, and operating cost evaluation. For capacity expansion, we used the screening curve approach (31, 32) because its computational efﬁciency enables evaluation of conventional generator economics over an entire year of demand and renewables production. Using screening curves enables us to easily explore different annual demand patterns. Our use of screening curves is a key point of comparison to other recent capacity expansion planning efforts, which limit cost evaluation to a small sample of time points for computational reasons (10, 11, 13, 16). Because screening curves cannot capture the time series aspects of VRE production, we used an investment step that precedes conventional capacity expansion. In this approach, based on refs. 33 and 34, VRE site selection is made on the basis of lowest levelized cost. This is consistent with an environment in which VRE project developers are not compensated for temporal value of VRE production and instead maximize capacity factor. VRE Site Selection and Levelized Costs. Following the methodology from refs. 33 and 34, we used modeled wind speeds at 80-m hub heights (35) and global horizontal irradiation data (36) to identify suitable areas for VRE development with thresholds for wind and solar resource quality and exclusions for protected areas, water bodies, and certain land use land cover types (agricultural land for solar, and forested land for both technologies). From these suitable areas, we created discrete potential project sites with a maximum area of 25 km 2, and applied land use factors of 7.5 MW/km 2 for solar PV and 2.25 MW/km 2 for

chunks.title: Least-Cost Targets for Renewable Energy in India
chunks.text: both technologies). From these suitable areas, we created discrete potential project sites with a maximum area of 25 km 2, and applied land use factors of 7.5 MW/km 2 for solar PV and 2.25 MW/km 2 for wind to estimate potential generation capacity and annual capacity factors. We then created 15 VRE build-out scenarios with three VRE installed capacity targets—200, 400, and 600 GW— each with ﬁve combinations of shares of solar PV and wind—0%–100% (all-wind), 25%–75% (more-wind), 50%–50% (balanced), 75%–25% (moresolar), and 100%–0% (all-solar). To meet individual wind and solar capacity targets for each VRE scenario, we selected sites with the highest annual capacity factors, limiting the selected capacity in each state to 15% to ensure spatial diversity. We estimated the levelized cost of VRE for each scenario assuming capital costs derived from India’s solar auctions (see SI Appendix, Table S2). For low levelized cost VRE scenarios, we assumed wind and solar PV capital costs to decline at 3% and 5% per year, respectively (23). We then created hourly generation proﬁles for each of the selected project sites from modeled wind (35) and solar (36) resource data for 2014, which captured the diurnal and seasonal weather patterns of wind and solar generation and formed the inputs to the capacity investment and system operation models (37); see SI Appendix, section 1. Future Demand Proﬁles. To create the 2030 hourly demand proﬁle, we linearly increased the 2014 hourly demand for India (38) to meet the energy demand forecast for 2030 (39). We then applied an adjustment across all time periods, linearly proportional to the demand in that period so that the 2030 time series matched both the 2030 annual peak demand and energy forecast (37). Employing renewable resource data and base electricity demand data from the same year maintained temporal correlation between weather and demand. We assume that the government of India forecast for energy demand includes growth in

We assume that the government of India forecast for energy demand includes growth in electricity access and agricultural and industrial demand. For urbanized demand proﬁles, we weighted and summed national, Delhi, and Mumbai hourly demands; seeSI Appendix, section 1 and Fig. S2. We also present a low electricity demand growth scenario in SI Appendix, section 2 (40). Conventional Capacity Investments. We considered three technologies for new conventional capacity—coal, CCGT, and CT. We assumed all new coal 6 of 8 | PNAS

We assumed CCGT and CT generators use imported liqueﬁed natural gas (LNG) [which is already increasing in India (41)] at USD 10 per MMBtu (42). We did not include nuclear or hydropower in new build-outs considered in the main scenarios, but we include proposed new build-outs in sensitivity scenarios presented in SI Appendix, section 2. We modeled pumped hydro capacity as hydro capacity with storage in our scenarios because existing capacity is less than 1% (2.6 GW) of total installed generation capacity (4). Operating this capacity as rechargeable storage would have effects on system operations similar to but less pronounced than the battery storage capacities considered in this paper. For battery storage scenarios, we exogenously added 15, 30, and 60 GW of 4-h battery storage, which is approximately 5%, 10%, and 20% of India’s expected peak demand in 2030. Further, we assumed a round-trip charge–discharge efﬁciency of 85%. Because results for all three capacities are qualitatively similar, we show results for only 60-GW storage capacity. Our capacity investment model proceeds in two steps: 1) net demand curve construction and 2) capacity

chunks.text: r all three capacities are qualitatively similar, we show results for only 60-GW storage capacity. Our capacity investment model proceeds in two steps: 1) net demand curve construction and 2) capacity investment decisions. To construct net demand curves, we used a simpliﬁed dispatch model to generate sequences of hydropower (storage) and battery operations. This model is similar to the linear economic dispatch model we used to compute generator economic dispatch described in the next section. The simpliﬁed dispatch model dispatches storage, hydro, and a simpliﬁed conventional generator with a convex cost curve and no constraints on maximum capacity or minimum operating level. Subtracting the resulting hydro and battery storage dispatch and must-run (run-of-river hydropower and nuclear) and VRE generation from demand in each hour gives the net demand proﬁle. To make conventional generator capacity investment decisions, we used a screening curve model (31, 32) with the net demand proﬁles. This approach assumes that generators are dispatched by marginal cost, and demand is inelastic. Generator costs, shown in detail in SI Appendix , Table S3, are described by ﬁxed costs (annualized capital costs and ﬁxed operations and maintenance [O&M] costs) and variable costs (fuel and variable O&M). Applying screening curves to the ﬁnal net demand proﬁles, we determined new capacities for coal, CCGT, and peaker CTs in 660-, 250-, and 200-MW increments, respectively. We assumed a reserve margin of 15% of annual peak load to ensure resource adequacy (43), and assigned this reserve margin to the CT, CCGT, and coal generators in proportion to their overall share. System Operation Costs. To compute total operating costs in each scenario, we developed a mixed-integer unit commitment and economic dispatch model in the Python-based open-source optimization modeling language (Pyomo) (44). The model optimally dispatches existing and new generators and storage over 24 h to meet demand for

chunks.title: Least-Cost Targets for Renewable Energy in India
chunks.text: economic dispatch model in the Python-based open-source optimization modeling language (Pyomo) (44). The model optimally dispatches existing and new generators and storage over 24 h to meet demand for each day of the year and determines realized VRE share in total generation, VRE curtailment, conventional generator plant load factors, emissions, and system operational costs. The objective functions of both net demand curve dispatch used in the capacity investment model and the full system economic dispatch models minimize the overall cost of generation and the cost of unserved energy. Formulations of both models are given in SI Appendix, section 1. We obtained variable costs and capacity for all existing generators from 2016 data ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3) and derived daily energy budgets and minimum generation levels for hydropower storage plants, and operating capacity factors of run-of-river hydropower and nuclear power plants from historical 2014 data (38, 45). We note that other papers also use similarly granular data on power plant costs, for example, refs. 46 and 47. Variability in variable costs of coal, gas, and diesel power plants reﬂects the heterogeneity in heat rates across plants. We assume constant heat rates across different loading levels for thermal power plants. Although hydropower storage plants may be able to reassign available energy potential across days and seasons depending upon the accuracy of forecasts for energy demand and other uses, we restrict the daily energy generation potential to historical generation levels. We assume an outage rate of 10% for all coal and gas generators. We did not include ramping constraints in our simpliﬁed model because even the most inﬂexible coal plants can ramp from a 55% minimum generation level to 100% of their rated capacity in 1 h (ramp rate of 1 MW per min), which is the temporal resolution of the model. We note that ramping capabilities of power plants may be a constraint at subhourly timescales and in

chunks.title: Least-Cost Targets for Renewable Energy in India
chunks.text: r rated capacity in 1 h (ramp rate of 1 MW per min), which is the temporal resolution of the model. We note that ramping capabilities of power plants may be a constraint at subhourly timescales and in transmission-constrained areas. Our model assumes a wellfunctioning, national electricity market with no transmission, political, or institutional constraints. We derive CO2 emissions factors of 0.63, 0.42, 0.92, and 0.82 tonnes-CO2 per MWh for CT, CCGT, coal, and diesel generators from average heat rates from the Central Electricity Authority (48) and fuel emissions intensities provided by the Energy Information Administration (49) (SI Appendix, Table S4). We note that these assumptions about emissions factors do not impact our core results on capacity expansion and dispatch, since these depend only on cost assumptions. However, any difference between our estimates of emissions factors and reality will pass through to estimates of ﬂeet-wide CO2 emissions. Data Availability. Wind resource data from Vaisala and demand, hydropower energy generation, and generator cost data from the Power Systems Operation Corporation of India are proprietary and can be accessed through those entities. Solar resource dataset is available from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory’s National Solar Radiation Database. Competition in Generative AI: Evidence from Consumer Demand Mark L. Egan, Dominic Russel, Claire Shi, and Vincent Yao NBER Working Paper No. 35953 October 2026 JEL No. D12, L13, O33 ABSTRACT How competitive will the market for generative AI be as it matures? Using novel transaction level credit and debit card data covering 174 million consumers and 114 billion transactions, we study the adoption of paid services and the demand-side foundations of competition in this market. As of April 2026, approximately 2.9% of U.S. consumers pay for at least one major generative AI service, with adoption highest among younger and higher-income consumers. Nearly all of these

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text:
is market. As of April 2026, approximately 2.9% of U.S. consumers pay for at least one major generative AI service, with adoption highest among younger and higher-income consumers. Nearly all of these paid users subscribe to basic plans that cost $30 or less per month. Three patterns suggest limited differentiation and low switching costs. First, although multihoming is common, it has declined as providers’ capabilities have expanded. Second, annual customer retention rates range from 20% to 45% across major AI providers, lower than those for many other subscription products. Third, switching rises around major model releases. Motivated by these findings, we develop and estimate a structural model of AI service demand and supply that reveals strong competitive pressure. Consumers are highly price sensitive, have much weaker preferences for particular providers than for AI overall, and view AI services as increasingly close substitutes. Our results suggest that, absent a substantial increase in AI model quality differentiation, growing substitutability among services will constrain providers’ pricing power and allow consumers to capture a large share of the surplus generated by these services. Mark L. Egan Harvard University Department of Economics and NBER megan@hbs.edu Dominic Russel Harvard University drussel@g.harvard.edu Claire Shi Harvard University cshi@g.harvard.edu Vincent Yao Georgia State University wyao2@gsu.edu

1 Introduction Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have the potential to transform economic activity and daily life. Since the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in late 2022 and Anthropic’s Claude in 2023, generative AI has rapidly become a prominent consumer technology used for a wide variety of everyday tasks, ranging from writing and coding to research and education. The adoption and pricing of these services, their effects on consumer welfare, and the valuations of AI firms will depend on how competitive the market becomes. A

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: and coding to research and education. The adoption and pricing of these services, their effects on consumer welfare, and the valuations of AI firms will depend on how competitive the market becomes. A central question is therefore whether providers of consumer-facing generative AI services can sustain market power as the market matures. The answer depends in part on consumer demand, particularly on how differentiated consumers perceive services to be and how readily they substitute one service for another. Yet, despite generative AI’s rapid growth and economic importance, systematic evidence on consumer demand and competition remains limited. In particular, little is known about who pays for these services, how consumers choose among providers, how persistent paid subscriptions are, whether services are substitutes or complements, and how responsive consumers are to changes in price and quality . This paper uses novel, de-identified transaction-level credit and debit card data to study consumer adoption of and demand for paid generative AI services. We first document how adoption varies across demographic groups and regions and how it has evolved over time. We then examine purchasing dynamics, including how long paid subscriptions persist, what leads consumers to switch providers, and whether they multihome. These patterns shed light on the degree of differentiation among services and consumers’ willingness to substitute across them— two demand-side forces that are critical to understanding competition, consumer welfare, and the market’s long-run structure. Motivated by these empirical patterns, we develop and estimate a structural model of AI service demand and supply . The demand side of the model builds on Gentzkow (2007) and uses the panel structure of our data to separately identify consumers’ preferences for individual services, the correlation in those preferences across services, and the incremental utility from subscribing to multiple services.

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: our data to separately identify consumers’ preferences for individual services, the correlation in those preferences across services, and the incremental utility from subscribing to multiple services. Distinguishing correlated preferences from complementarity is important. A consumer may subscribe to both OpenAI and Anthropic products because of a strong general taste for AI, or because they are complements so that subscribing to one raises the value of the other. These features of demand have distinct implications for competition. We use the estimated model to quantify how these forces shape market power, measure the surplus generated by AI services and its division between consumers and providers, and examine how changes in market structure affect competition. Overall, our reduced-form and structural results point to strong demand-side competitive pressure in the market for consumer AI services. Consumers differ substantially in their overall taste for AI, but provider-specific tastes are small relative to this common component: for instance, consumers who value an OpenAI product also tend to value an Anthropic product. Moreover, as model capabilities have expanded and converged, consumers increasingly treat these services as substitutes. Access to one service is therefore less valuable to a consumer who already has access to another. Together with consumers’ price sensitivity , these patterns leave providers with limited scope to sustain market power through provider-specific preferences. Although consumers’ sensitivity to model quality could give a provider market power if it achieves a level of quality that rivals cannot match, frontier model capabilities have thus far converged across providers. Absent a reversal of this pattern, our results suggest that the demand side is unlikely to support sustained market power and that, ultimately , consumers will capture a large share of the surplus generated by generative AI products. Our transaction-level sample spans

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: nd side is unlikely to support sustained market power and that, ultimately , consumers will capture a large share of the surplus generated by generative AI products. Our transaction-level sample spans January 2021 through April 2026 and contains 174 million consumers and 114 billion transactions. Transaction descriptors allow us to identify payments to major AI providers. We focus primarily on the four large generative AI providers observed in our data: Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), OpenAI (ChatGPT), and xAI (Grok). For each transaction, we observe the date and amount, together with anonymized identifiers for the card and consumer. These data allow us to construct a panel that tracks consumers’ purchases over time and across AI providers. We also observe demographic information, including consumers’ ages, incomes, and regions. We focus on paid consumer adoption, excluding both free AI subscriptions and enterprise adoption. Unlike free subscriptions, paid AI subscriptions reflect providers’ ability to monetize consumer demand, and are a core source of their revenue. For OpenAI, consumer subscriptions account for approximately 75% of revenue in 2024 and 60% at the beginning of 2026. Even Anthropic, which has traditionally targeted enterprise customers, generates approximately 20% of its revenue from consumer sales.1 Consumer subscriptions may also be especially important for future improvements in model quality , since AI companies generally do not train models on enterprise data. We use the data to document several new facts about consumer adoption of paid AI services. First, paid adoption has grown but remains relatively limited in the United States. In April 2026, 2.9% of consumers paid for at least one product from one of the four major AI providers in our sample, in line with recent industry estimates.2 OpenAI was the most widely adopted provider, with 2.4% of consumers paying for an OpenAI product. Although the share of consumers paying for Anthropic

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: sample, in line with recent industry estimates.2 OpenAI was the most widely adopted provider, with 2.4% of consumers paying for an OpenAI product. Although the share of consumers paying for Anthropic products had grown in recent months, it remained at only 0.5% in April 2026. Paid adoption is substantially more common among younger and higher-income consumers: those earning more than $200,000 per year are 1.7 times as likely to pay as those earning less than $50,000, and those younger than 55 are 1.8 times as likely as those aged 55 or older. These relationships between demographics and adoption hold broadly across AI providers. We also 1See estimates from Gavin (2026); Parham (2026); Lin (2025). 2See, for example, Bank of America Institute (2026); PNC Economics Research (2026). document meaningful geographic variation, with adoption highest in California, Washington, and the Mid-Atlantic region. Second, consumers frequently multihome across AI providers, particularly during the earlier part of our sample. For example, roughly 45% of consumers who paid for an Anthropic product also paid for an OpenAI product in June 2024. However, the prevalence of multihoming has declined over time. By April 2026, less than 30% of consumers who paid for an Anthropic product also paid for an OpenAI product. This decline is consistent with AI services becoming less complementary as providers have developed increasingly general-purpose products with overlapping capabilities. Third, retention among paying customers is low, especially relative to other subscription products such as newspapers and streaming services. We measure retention by following a consumer’s first observed purchase from an AI provider. Retention varies across providers and is highest for OpenAI: after 12 months, roughly 45% of OpenAI users remain subscribed, compared with 30% of Anthropic users. By comparison, annual retention rates for Netflix and Spotify in our data are around 70%. Fourth, consumers switch

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: roughly 45% of OpenAI users remain subscribed, compared with 30% of Anthropic users. By comparison, annual retention rates for Netflix and Spotify in our data are around 70%. Fourth, consumers switch across providers, and switching activity increases following major model releases. We measure model capabilities using data from the Epoch Capabilities Index (Epoch AI, 2025). When Anthropic or OpenAI releases an improved model, the share of consumers who paid only for the rival in the previous month and begin paying for the provider with the model improvement rises by about 25%. Taken together, these facts describe a growing market characterized by limited customer loyalty and services that appear increasingly substitutable. If these patterns persist, they suggest that the market for AI services will likely be highly competitive and it will be challenging for providers to sustain market power in the long run. Motivated by these reduced-form facts, we develop and estimate a structural model of demand for AI services to better understand consumer preferences, how those preferences have evolved over time, the resulting welfare consequences, and the implications for market structure. Following Gentzkow (2007), we model consumer choice as a discrete-choice problem in which consumers choose among bundles of AI services rather than necessarily selecting a single service. The model allows consumers to purchase multiple services simultaneously and permits pairs of services to be either complements or substitutes. We allow consumers to have heterogeneous and correlated preferences across AI services in the spirit of Berryet al.(1995) and Berryet al.(2004). Distinguishing preference heterogeneity from complementarity is particularly important given that either force can explain the prevalence of multihoming. For example, a consumer who places a high value on Anthropic’s Claude may also place a high value on OpenAI’s ChatGPT because the consumer has a strong general preference

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: he prevalence of multihoming. For example, a consumer who places a high value on Anthropic’s Claude may also place a high value on OpenAI’s ChatGPT because the consumer has a strong general preference for AI services, even if the two services are substitutes. Alternatively , the services may be complements, such that subscribing to Claude increases the value of subscribing to ChatGPT. On the supply side, we assume that AI providers compete in a differentiated-products Bertrand–Nash price-setting game. Providers recognize that consumers may purchase bundles containing products from multiple firms and that the price of one product can therefore affect demand for other products. When products are substitutes, a price increase by one provider shifts demand toward its competitors. When products are complements, a price increase can reduce demand for both products. Thus, greater substitutability intensifies price competition, whereas greater complementarity softens competition and supports higher equilibrium prices. We also consider a dynamic extension with learning by doing on the supply side. Specifically , we allow future model capabilities to depend on the number of users a provider attracts today , reflecting the idea that a larger user base gives the provider access to more data or resources that can be used to improve model quality (Prufer and Schottmüller, 2021; Hagiu and Wright, 2023). This force creates a dynamic incentive to set lower prices today: lower prices attract more users, improving future model quality and raising future demand. We estimate the demand model by maximum likelihood using our transaction-level panel data on consumer purchase decisions. The panel structure is central to separately identifying persistent heterogeneity in consumer preferences, correlations in preferences across providers, and complementarity or substitutability between AI services. Repeated purchase decisions and switching patterns identify persistent differences in

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: rences, correlations in preferences across providers, and complementarity or substitutability between AI services. Repeated purchase decisions and switching patterns identify persistent differences in consumers’ preferences. Correlated purchase behavior across providers helps identify correlations in preferences, while, conditional on those preferences, consumers’ tendency to multihome rather than switch between services helps identify whether the services are complements or substitutes. Our structural estimates on the demand side provide insight into the nature of consumer preferences and how they have evolved over time. To begin, consumer demand for AI services is relatively price elastic, with an average own-price elasticity of about -4.6. In our model, this high elasticity implies relatively little horizontal differentiation across AI providers and thus limited market power for providers. Our estimates of consumer preference heterogeneity reinforce the conclusion of limited horizontal differentiation. Although preferences vary substantially across consumers, consumerspecific preferences are strongly correlated across AI providers: consumers who value one provider more than average also tend to highly value other providers. For example, the estimated correlation between consumer-specific preferences for OpenAI and Anthropic products is 0.89. The lowest preference correlation between any pair of products is OpenAI and Google, at 0.55, which is still substantial. These estimates suggest that providers largely appeal to the same consumers and that provider-specific preferences account for relatively little of the variation in demand. Despite this limited horizontal differentiation, we find some degree of vertical differentiation across providers, consistent with observed market shares. At the end of our sample, the average consumer was willing to pay a $10 monthly premium for OpenAI products relative to Anthropic products. Part of this difference reflects model

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: served market shares. At the end of our sample, the average consumer was willing to pay a $10 monthly premium for OpenAI products relative to Anthropic products. Part of this difference reflects model quality: our estimates indicate that consumers are willing to pay more for higher-quality models. For instance, moving from GPT- 4’s capability level to GPT-5.5 Pro’s raises average willingness to pay for OpenAI products by approximately $25 per month. Finally , we generally find that consumers increasingly view AI services as substitutes, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic products. As the capabilities of these services have expanded and converged, the incremental value of subscribing to one service for a consumer who already subscribes to the other has declined. This evolution is consistent with the observed decline in multihoming and has important implications for competition and the long-run structure of the consumer AI market. In sum, our demand estimates point to three sources of competitive pressure: limited horizontal differentiation, strong substitution in response to quality improvements, and the declining incremental value of additional subscriptions. Under differentiatedproducts Bertrand–Nash pricing, these forces put downward pressure on equilibrium markups. We then use our demand estimates to calibrate the supply side of the model. We estimate markups, expressed as a share of the price (i.e., Lerner Index) ranging from 19% to 59% across products, suggesting that about 41-81% of revenues are used to cover the marginal costs of running these AI models. In our dynamic extension with endogenous improvements in model quality , we find even lower markups. In particular, when providers internalize the future value of expanding their user bases, the marginal cost of operating a typical service is roughly 70% to 80% of its subscription price. These estimates capture the variable marginal costs of providing AI services but exclude fixed operating costs and

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: cost of operating a typical service is roughly 70% to 80% of its subscription price. These estimates capture the variable marginal costs of providing AI services but exclude fixed operating costs and expenditures on research and model development. Thus, they are an upper bound on total profitability . The model also allows us to conduct counterfactual analyses and quantify the consumer surplus generated by paid AI services. We estimate that access to paid AI subscriptions generates average consumer surplus of approximately $1.09 per consumer per quarter. This average masks substantial heterogeneity because most consumers do not currently subscribe to an AI service. Among adopters, paid AI services generate average consumer surplus of approximately $35 each quarter, over and above the amount spent on AI subscriptions. We also use the model to examine how consumer preferences for AI services shape competition. We begin by considering substitutability across services. By the end of our sample, all pairs of AI services are substitutes on average: the marginal utility of an additional subscription is lower for a consumer who already subscribes to another service. For some services, such as Anthropic which is very substitutable with OpenAI, equilibrium prices would be 30% higher under a counterfactual with no substitutability , and up to 60% higher if the services were complements, as several service pairs were early in our sample. The strong correlation in consumers’ preferences across providers also constrains markups by limiting product differentiation. In a counterfactual in which preferences across providers are uncorrelated, and services are therefore more differentiated, equilibrium prices are approximately 2% to 10% higher. Finally , we examine Anthropic’s effect on competition. Although OpenAI remains the dominant provider, Anthropic has grown rapidly from a small base since the release of Claude Code. To quantify Anthropic’s competitive role, we consider a

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: t on competition. Although OpenAI remains the dominant provider, Anthropic has grown rapidly from a small base since the release of Claude Code. To quantify Anthropic’s competitive role, we consider a counterfactual in which Anthropic is removed from the market. Because consumers’ preferences for the two providers’ services are highly correlated and the services are strong substitutes, Anthropic exerts meaningful competitive discipline on OpenAI. In the counterfactual, OpenAI would raise its prices modestly , but sufficiently that its equilibrium market share would fall relative to its market share in the baseline scenario when it competes with Anthropic. The joint price and adoption response is consistent with Anthropic constraining OpenAI’s exercise of market power. Accounting for the fact that other providers change prices in response to entry amplifies the welfare gain of having Anthropic in the market by 21%, to $5.05 per quarter per AI user. Taken together, our results provide new evidence on consumer demand for generative AI services. Despite AI’s prominence in public discourse, paid consumer adoption remains modest, although recent trends suggest that it will continue to grow rapidly . The limited persistence of paid subscriptions, correlation in preferences, and the shift from complementarity toward substitutability have important implications for the diffusion of AI services and the industry’s long-run competitive structure. Related Literature Our paper contributes to a rapidly growing literature on the adoption and use of generative AI. Recent evidence suggests that exposure to generative AI is now common among both consumers and workers. Survey estimates (e.g., Bicket al., 2026a; Gottfriedet al., 2026a) show that around half of U.S. adults have used generative AI, and that around a quarter to half of U.S. employees have used generative AI for work (e.g., Bicket al., 2026c; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 2026; Kemp, 2025; Bicket al.,

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: ative AI, and that around a quarter to half of U.S. employees have used generative AI for work (e.g., Bicket al., 2026c; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 2026; Kemp, 2025; Bicket al., 2026b). AI adoption for business tasks is also growing inside the firm (Bonneyet al., 2026), and at the executive level (Yotzovet al., 2026). Our analysis complements these survey-based studies by using transaction-level panel data to identify payments to specific AI providers and follow the same consumers over time. This allows us to study provider-specific adoption, multihoming, switching, and retention, and their implications for competition. Our measure is also deliberately narrower than survey-based measures which capture free and enterprise use. Others use non-survey data to study AI adoption. Among these, descriptive industry reports (Bank of America Institute, 2026; PNC Economics Research, 2026) are the closest to our use of transaction-level data. Using aggregated Bank of America data, Bank of America Institute (2026) reports that roughly 3% of households pay for AI services and that paid adoption is concentrated among younger and higher-income households, consistent with our first descrip- tive findings. Demireret al.(2025) use API usage data from OpenRouter and Microsoft Azure (platforms primarily serving developers and technology firms) to document rapid entry , falling prices, and frequent turnover among leading LLMs. We find similar evidence of substantial competitive pressure in the consumer AI market. Caoui (2026) uses data from LMArena, where users choose between anonymized LLM responses, to study preferences over model capabilities and response styles. Data from AI providers have also been used to analyze how consumers use AI products: for example, Chatterjiet al.(2025) and Handaet al.(2025) find that writing, information, and software development are particularly common use cases. Second, we contribute to emerging work quantifying the impacts and

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: atterjiet al.(2025) and Handaet al.(2025) find that writing, information, and software development are particularly common use cases. Second, we contribute to emerging work quantifying the impacts and value of generative AI. Most closely related is Brynjolfssonet al.(2026) who use online choice experiments to elicit the compensation consumers would require to give up access to generative AI chatbot tools for one month. In March 2026, they estimate a mean willingness to accept of $124.50 per month and a median willingness to accept of $11.40. Their welfare object is complementary , but different from ours. Their estimates capture the value of access to generative AI tools, including services available without a paid subscription, whereas we estimate the incremental surplus generated by paid products relative to an outside option that may include free or employer-provided access. More broadly , we relate to a number of recent works that study the effects of AI tools on economic outcomes such as productivity and firm performance (e.g., Noy and Zhang, 2023; Chen and Chan, 2024; Cuiet al., 2024; Chen and Stratton, 2026; Otiset al., 2024; Dillonet al., 2025; Songet al., 2026; Sarkar, 2025; Brynjolfssonet al., 2025; Hampoleet al., 2025; Babina et al., 2026), as well as the impact of consumers delegating purchase choices (e.g., Delaprez and Hortaçsu, 2026) and financial decision-making (e.g., Choukhmaneet al., 2026; Luet al., 2025). Building on this literature, we study the welfare implications of AI market structure, complementing existing work on the potential welfare impact of increased productivity , worker displacement, or changes in economic behavior (e.g., Athey and Morton, 2025). Finally , our paper relates to the industrial organization literature on demand estimation, new products, and consumer welfare (Berryet al., 1995, 2004; Nevo, 2000). Petrin (2002) demonstrates how demand-estimation methods and consumer-level information can be used to quantify the welfare

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: n, new products, and consumer welfare (Berryet al., 1995, 2004; Nevo, 2000). Petrin (2002) demonstrates how demand-estimation methods and consumer-level information can be used to quantify the welfare gains generated by a new product, focusing on the introduction of the minivan. Our model is most closely related to Gentzkow (2007), who develops a demand model that allows for both heterogeneity in consumer preferences and complementarity across products to value online newspapers, and the broader demand estimation literature that allows for complementarity between products (Hendel, 1999; Dubé, 2004; Thomassenet al., 2017; Allen and Rehbeck, 2019; Compiani, 2022; Iaria and Wang, 2020; Wang, 2024; Ershovet al., 2025). We adapt the framework from Gentzkow (2007) to the rapidly evolving market for subscription AI services and use panel data to separately identify persistent preference heterogeneity and complementarities across providers. We extend the framework by allowing both to evolve over time, and connect the demand estimates to equilibrium price competition. These features allow us to quantify the surplus generated by paid AI services and study how changing relationships among providers affect competition and the industry’s long-run structure. 2 Data Our main data is a panel of anonymized credit and debit card transactions from Fiserv, a leading provider of payments and financial services technology solutions. Our sample covers January 2021 through April 2026 and includes information on 114 billion transactions from 719 million cards and 174 million consumers. To limit our sample to instances in which we likely observe individuals’ primary cards, our baseline sample restricts to individual-months with at least 20 transactions. This restriction reduces our sample to 82 million consumers. The transaction-level data allow us to study within-consumer purchasing patterns over time and across products. This, in turn, enables us to provide novel evidence on competition

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: 82 million consumers. The transaction-level data allow us to study within-consumer purchasing patterns over time and across products. This, in turn, enables us to provide novel evidence on competition and substitution among AI products. For each transaction, we observe the purchase date and amount; anonymized card and cardholder identifiers; and the merchant’s name, industry , and location. The data also include consumer demographics, such as age, income group, and ZIP code. Table 1 reports summary statistics for our sample of consumers. In January 2026, consumers in our sample made an average of 63 transactions and spent an average of $3,268 over the month. The sample spans the income distribution: 15% of consumers have annual incomes below $50,000, while 16% have incomes above $200,000. It also covers all age groups, with 46% of consumers aged 55 or older and 9% aged 34 or younger. We identify AI-related transactions primarily using merchant names (Appendix A.1 includes additional details). We focus on the four large generative AI providers observed in our data: Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), OpenAI (ChatGPT), and xAI (Grok). Our analysis is restricted to paid consumer accounts, which capture realized consumer demand and provide revealed-preference evidence of consumers’ willingness to pay . They also measure a key source of revenue for providers. Our data do not capture free consumer accounts or enterprise accounts. For some analyses, we also identify transactions for a number of other subscription products, including Grammarly , Chegg, Netflix, Spotify , and the New York Times. Other Data Sources.We obtain model-capability measures from the Epoch AI Capabilities Index, which assesses performance across a broad range of tasks (Epoch AI, 2025). Figure 1a plots the index for each provider’s frontier model over time. Model capabilities vary substantially over time but relatively little across providers at a given date, showing that AI providers’ frontier

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: lots the index for each provider’s frontier model over time. Model capabilities vary substantially over time but relatively little across providers at a given date, showing that AI providers’ frontier models have thus far advanced at similar rates. We collect product prices from company announcements and archived webpages. We focus on each company’s core entry-level product, which is priced between $19.99 and $30 per month for each provider throughout our sample. Figure 1b shows that, across all providers, the vast majority of those who pay for a product in our data pay less than $35 per month, consistent with the dominance of these entry-level products. 3 Motivating Evidence: AI Adoption, Multihoming, and Churn To begin examining the competitive dynamics of the consumer AI industry , we document several new facts about paid AI adoption. We find that multihoming is common but has declined over time, that churn is high relative to other subscription products, and that consumers are particularly likely to move across providers around model releases. These facts motivate and discipline the model developed in Section 4. 3.1 Patterns of AI Adoption Overall Trends.Consumer use of paid AI products has grown over time, although adoption has varied across providers. Figure 1c shows that by April 2026, 2.9% of consumers paid for at least one of the four major AI products in our sample. Scaling by the number of U.S. credit card holders implies that over 6 million individuals paid for a consumer AI service that month— roughly equal to the combined subscriber bases of the Wall Street Journal and The Economist, or about two-thirds the size of YouTube TV’s subscriber base. OpenAI accounted for the largest share, with 2.4% of all consumers subscribing. Anthropic, however, experienced particularly rapid growth following the release of Claude 4.6 in February 2026: the share of purchasers tripled from January 2026 to April 2026. The Geography of Paid AI Adoption.Figure 2 maps paid

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: ed particularly rapid growth following the release of Claude 4.6 in February 2026: the share of purchasers tripled from January 2026 to April 2026. The Geography of Paid AI Adoption.Figure 2 maps paid consumer AI adoption as of April 2026. Adoption is highest along the coasts and in major metropolitan areas: California, Washington, Florida, and the Mid-Atlantic exhibit particularly high rates of AI adoption. By contrast, adoption is much lower in less densely populated areas in the South and Midwest. Appendix Figures C.1 and C.2 show more localized adoption patterns within Massachusetts and New York City . In Massachusetts, usage is concentrated in the Boston area, reaching as high as 38% in ZIP code 02163 which includes Harvard Business School and its on-campus housing. In New York City , usage is highest in Manhattan—particularly lower and central Manhattan— and northwestern Brooklyn, with a sharp drop-off in the Bronx and in outer Queens and Brooklyn. Appendix Figure C.3 compares paid AI adoption across different products in the 50 largest commuting zones. Panel (a) shows that OpenAI and Anthropic have very similar spatial patterns, with adoption especially high in San Francisco, Washington, DC, and Austin and lower in Midwestern cities such as Cleveland and St. Louis. Panel (b) shows a similar relationship for xAI, although xAI adoption is relatively less concentrated in the Mid-Atlantic and more concentrated in parts of the South and Southwest, including Austin, Phoenix, and Jacksonville. Paid AI Adoption by Demographics.Rates of paid AI adoption also differ sharply across demographic groups. Many consumers pay for more than one AI product in a given month, though multihoming has declined over time. These patterns help identify substitutability over time in the model. Multihoming at OpenAI and Anthropic.To begin, Figure 4a focuses on the two most popular providers as of April 2026, OpenAI and Anthropic. However, their spending in other categories does not appear to strongly differ from that of matched non-adopters. 4 Model Motivated by our empirical evidence, in this section, we develop a structural model of demand for paid AI services. The model allows us to characterize consumer preferences, their change over time, and implications for market competition. We then use the model to study the equilibrium structure of the consumer AI market and

We then use the model to study the equilibrium structure of the consumer AI market and implications of competition on welfare. 4.1 Setup We model consumers’ decisions about which AI services to use as a discrete choice problem in which consumers may choose bundles of services rather than a single service. Our results in Section 3.2 show that consumers frequently multihome across providers. Following Gentzkow (2007), our model distinguishes between two explanations for this multihoming. First, services may be complements, so that combinations of providers are more valuable than the sum of their individual components. Second, multihoming may reflect correlated preference heterogeneity , whereby consumers who strongly prefer one provider also tend to prefer others. Each consumerichooses a bundle of AI services from the set of servicesJ= 1, . . . , J. For tractability , we restrict consumers to choosing at most two services. The choice setCtherefore consists of the outside option, theJindividual services, and the �J  two-service bundles. We let c∈ Cdenote a bundle and let|c|denote the number of services contained in bundlec. Under our restriction,|c| ∈0,1,2. 4.2 Utility Consumer preferences over AI services are heterogeneous. It consists of a price component,−αp jt withα >0, observed service characteristicsX jt, and an unobserved quality componentξ jt. The vectorX jt contains observable service characteristics, such as measures of model quality or capability , whileξjt captures service attributes observed by consumers but not by the econometrician. We allow tastes for services offered by different providers to be correlated within a consumer, so that multihoming may arise from correlated preference heterogeneity rather than complementarities between services. We assume that these tastes remain fixed over time. The termsΓ ct andγ ic capture bundle-specific utility that arises when consumers use multiple AI services. We normalize these terms to zero for the outside option and all single-service bundles: Γct =γ ic = 0for allc∈ Csuch that|c| ≤1. Thus,Γ ct andγ ic are only relevant for two-service bundles. The termΓ ct captures the average utility associated with bundlecat timet, whileγ ic captures consumer-specific heterogeneity in preferences for that bundle. AllowingΓ ct to vary across bundles and over time permits complementarities between services to evolve as AI technologies and consumer use cases change. Positive values ofΓ ct +γ ic imply that consumeriderives additional utility from consuming the services in bundlecjointly beyond the sum of their standalone utilities, while negative values imply that the services are substitutes. Finally ,νict is a consumer-bundle-time-specific utility shock. This term captures transitory factors that affect service choices and rationalizes why consumers do not always choose the same bundle over time. In our baseline analysis, we assume providers play a static differentiated-product Bertrand pricing game. We then extend the model to account for dynamic learning by doing incentives. Thus, despite consumers choosing bundles rather than individual services, the equilibrium markup takes the same form as in the standard Bertrand pricing model. The key difference is that the relevant demand elasticity is computed from product demand, which aggregates substitution across all bundles containing servicej. Complementarities enter through the bundle demand system: bundle-specific utility affects the bundle choice probabilities, which in turn determine product demand and its price elasticity . An important implication of the model is that the degree of complementarity between services directly influences firms’ pricing decisions. For example, suppose servicesjandkbecome less complementary (or, equivalently , more substitutable) over time, so thatΓ jkt decreases. Holding all else constant, consumers become less likely to purchase the bundle{j, k}, reducing demand for both services. As a result, providerjfinds it optimal to lower its price. More generally , changes in complementarities affect equilibrium prices through their impact on product demand and its price elasticity . 4.5 Extension: Dynamic Model Quality In our baseline version of the model, firms set prices to compete for consumers, taking product quality as fixed. However, we also consider an extension in which product quality evolves over time and depends, in part, on past adoption. Specifically , we introduce learning by doing, whereby providers improve their products as they accumulate users. This mechanism differs slightly from the traditional learning-by-doing framework, in which accumulated experience lowers the marginal cost of production. In our setting, learning by doing instead improves product quality . This extension allows us to study how competition affects not only current prices and adoption, but also the evolution of future product quality . Consumer Demand.Letω jt denote the quality of providerj’s model at timet. Model quality is one of the observed characteristics contained inX jt and therefore directly affects consumer utility through equation (3). Letβ ω >0denote the marginal utility of model quality . Thus, all else equal, improvements in model quality increase current demand. Because current demand determines the number of users from whom a provider learns, higher quality today can increase adoption, which in turn improves future product quality and future demand. The termϕ t captures changes in the state of AI technology that are common across providers, whileη jt is an idiosyncratic model-quality productivity shock. Dynamic Pricing.Because current demand affects future product quality , the link between adoption and learning makes the provider’s pricing problem dynamic. Given current model qualitiesω t, providers choose prices to maximize the present discounted value of profits. Let Vj(ωt)denote providerj’s value function. Providerjsolves Vj(ωt) = maxpjt {sjt(pjt −κ jt) +ϱE t [Vj(ωt+1)]},(14) whereϱ∈(0,1)denotes the provider’s discount factor. In this framework, providers recognize that their pricing decisions affect the allocation of consumers across providers and, through learning by doing, the future quality of all products in the market. In particular, a lower price for providerjincreases its own current demand and therefore its future product quality , while also shifting demand away from competing providers and reducing the experience from which those providers learn. Providers internalize both effects when setting prices. The second term captures the dynamic value of changing the allocation of users across providers through its effect on future model quality . A change in providerj’s price affects not only its own user base and future quality , but also the user bases and future qualities of competing providers. The own-quality component of the dynamic term gives providers an incentive to lower current prices in order to attract users and improve their future products. At the same time, a lower price can reduce competitors’ future quality by shifting users away from them, providing an additional strategic incentive to compete for users today . When there is no learning by doing (λ= 0), these dynamic incentives disappear and the pricing condition collapses to the static pricing condition in equation (12). 5 Estimation We estimate the demand model in two steps. First, we recover consumer preferences via maximum likelihood using panel data on consumer adoption patterns. The estimation identifies the joint distribution of consumer preferences over product characteristics. The panel structure—using repeated observations for a given consumer over time—is valuable for identifying persistent consumer heterogeneity , while substitution patterns over time identify the correlation in unobserved tastes across products and substitutability of products. Second, we relate the estimated preference parameters to observable product characteristics, such as price and model quality , to quantify the sources of consumer heterogeneity . We then calibrate the supply side of the model. Combining the demand-side estimates with the providers’ first-order conditions allows us to recover each provider’s marginal cost parameters. Later, we will conduct counterfactuals with our demand-side estimates to study implications of competition on prices and welfare. 5.1 Distribution of Heterogeneous Preferences Consumers’ preferences in equation (2) include a common time- and service-varying component,δ jt; a heterogeneous individual- and service-specific component,θ ij; a common

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: of Heterogeneous Preferences Consumers’ preferences in equation (2) include a common time- and service-varying component,δ jt; a heterogeneous individual- and service-specific component,θ ij; a common time- and bundle-varying component,Γ ct; and a heterogeneous individual- and bundle-specific component,γ ic. Here, we describe how we parameterize the heterogeneity in consumers’ preferences, θij andγ ic. We allow consumers’ preferences and the degree of complementarity and substitutability across AI services to be heterogeneous and correlated. We assume that consumers’ persistent preference heterogeneity ,(θi,γ i), follows a multivariate normal distribution: θi i.i.d.∼ N(0,Σ θ),γ i i.i.d.∼ N(0,Σ γ),(16) The vectorθ i captures heterogeneous preferences for individual AI services, whileγ i captures heterogeneous preferences for service bundles. We allow preferences for individual services to be correlated within a consumer, so the covariance matrixΣθ is unrestricted. For tractability , we assume that preferences for service bundles are independent across bundles and independent of service-specific preferences: Σγ = diag � σ2γ,cc∈C2 ,Cov �θi,γ i =0.(17) Allowing for both persistent preference heterogeneity and bundle-specific utility flows enables the model to distinguish between two explanations for the multihoming observed in the data. Consumers may adopt multiple AI services because the services are complements—for example, because ChatGPT increases the value of Claude—or because consumers with strong preferences for one service also tend to have strong preferences for the other. The first mechanism is captured by the bundle-specific preference terms, while the second is captured by correlation in consumers’ service-specific preferences. 5.2 Demand Estimation Maximum Likelihood Estimation.We estimate the model by maximum likelihood using our quarterly panel of individual bundle choices over the period 2024Q1-2026Q1. Implementation Details.We estimate the model on individuals who have at least 20 transactions in each of the nine quarters from 2024Q1-2026Q1 (T= 1, . . . ,8from 2024Q2-2026Q1 taking initial shares in 2024Q1 as given). A consumer is classified as having adopted the AI bundle in quartertif they used all the products in that bundle at any point in the quarter. We focus on the four largest AI providers in our data (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Google) and allow multi-homing up to two products, so there arec= 10possible bundles that are non-empty . 5 As a result, there are 96 parameters which we estimate iteratively using L-BFGS with increasingly lower tolerance. In particular, we estimate average preference heterogeneityδ jt (4×8), the lower-diagonal of its variance-covariance matrixΣ θ (10), complementarities from using multiple AI servicesΓ ct (6×8), and its diagonal variance matrixΣ γ (6). To isolate this variation, we instrument for price using a dummy equal to one for xAI observations from Q1 2025 onward — the period following 5In our sample, fewer than 0.05% of consumers have ever used more than two products. xAI’s price increase from $16 to $30 per month.6 5.2.2 Identification The parameters are identified from consumers’ observed choice behavior. While all parameters are jointly identified in the model, it is useful to provide intuition for the patterns in the data that are most informative about each set of parameters. The mean utility terms,δ jt andΓ ct, are identified primarily from average choice frequencies. For example, if ChatGPT has a large market share, this implies a high value ofδ ChatGPT,t. Similarly , if the ChatGPT–Claude bundle is chosen more frequently than would be predicted based on the individual market shares of ChatGPT and Claude, this suggests a higher value of Γct, all else equal. The distribution of preference heterogeneity ,(Σ θ,Σ γ), is identified from persistent withinconsumer choice behavior. For example, if a consumer repeatedly chooses ChatGPT over time, this persistence cannot be fully explained byδ jt becauseδ jt is common across consumers. Instead, such behavior is indicative of persistent heterogeneity in preferences. More generally , the diagonal elements ofΣ θ andΣ γ are identified from the extent to which consumers repeatedly make similar choices over time. The off-diagonal elements ofΣ θ are identified from co-adoption and substitution patterns across

chunks.title: Competition in Generative AI: Consumer Demand
chunks.text: Σ θ andΣ γ are identified from the extent to which consumers repeatedly make similar choices over time. The off-diagonal elements ofΣ θ are identified from co-adoption and substitution patterns across AI services. For example, if consumers who currently use or previously used Claude are systematically more likely to adopt ChatGPT, this implies a positive covariance between preferences for the two services, i.e., Cov(θi,ChatGPT, θi,Claude)>0.(22) Empirically , a central challenge is separating the interaction terms,Γct, from correlated preference heterogeneity ,(Σθ,Σ γ). For example, frequent selection of the ChatGPT-Claude bundle could indicate that the products are complements, but could also reflect persistent unobserved heterogeneity: some consumers may simply have high demand for AI products. We distinguish these channels using panel variation, following the logic of Gentzkow (2007). The key identifying assumption is that the correlated component of unobserved preferences is persistent over time. Under this assumption, if two AI products are complements, a consumer should be more likely to use both products in the same periods and neither in others. By contrast, if multi-homing is driven by correlated taste heterogeneity , high-AI-type consumers will have persistently high demand for AI tools, but may switch between single-homing and multi-homing as relative product quality changes, including around model releases, as suggested by Figure 6. 6In December 2024, xAI raised prices of Premium+ from $16 to $22. In February 2025, after the release of Grok 3, they introduced SuperGrok at $30 and raised the price of Premium+ to $40 (see, e.g., Mehta, 2025). 5.3 Supply Calibration Using the estimated parameters, observed market shares and prices, and the providers’ firstorder conditions (eq. 12), we calibrate the supply side of the model, which consists of the providers’ marginal costs of providing AI services,κ jt. Our estimates are an upper bound on profitability as they ignore fixed operating costs and research and development expenditures. 7 Counterfactuals and Implications for Competition We use our model to examine how product substitutability and preference heterogeneity shape competition. We find that equilibrium prices would be substantially higher if AI products were, on average, complements rather than substitutes or if consumers’ preferences across products were independent rather than positively correlated. Because Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s products are particularly close substitutes and consumers’ preferences for them are highly correlated, Anthropic plays an important role in constraining market power despite its relatively small current market share. A counterfactual without Anthropic indicates that a meaningful share of the resulting welfare loss comes from higher prices charged by the remaining providers (in addition to the direct loss of access to Anthropic’s products). 7.1 Effects of Substitutability on Competition The increased substitutability between AI products has several important implications for market structure. As in Gentzkow (2007), even though multihoming rates are unconditionally high, our model suggests that this is largely from correlated preference heterogeneity rather than AI products exhibiting strong complementarities. To illustrate the impact of substitutability on prices and market shares, we consider a counterfactual in 2026Q1 whereΓ counter = 0and Γcounter =|Γ|. Without substitutability , consumers respond by being more likely to bundle AI products together. This increases the share of consumers using AI, but providers dampen this effect by raising prices since

This increases the share of consumers using AI, but providers dampen this effect by raising prices since there is more market power. Table 5 shows that ifΓ = 0, prices would be higher for all providers, and in net, shares of most providers would be higher than the baseline (Figure 8 plots counterfactual shares over time). Anthropic is a particularly interesting case. In this counterfactual, Anthropic raises their prices from $20 per month to $26 per month. However, even with this price change, Anthropic’s market share nearly doubles, from 0.50% to 0.96%. OpenAI, GoogleAI and xAI experience smaller changes in prices and shares. The disproportionate increase in Anthropic’s market shares and prices are likely because OpenAI (which has the largest baseline market share) is by far the most substitutable with Anthropic:Γ OpenAI, Anthropic = -6.44, compared with ΓOpenAI, Google = -0.90 andΓ OpenAI, xAI = -0.04. Our results are stronger if AI products were all complements rather than neither complements nor substitutes. Relative to the baseline, we find that with|Γ|, providers increase their prices by $6-$12 per month. The share of consumers paying for OpenAI and Anthropic rises to 3.02% and 2.33%, respectively , representing a percentage increase of 16% and 364%. Overall, these results suggest that as AI providers have evolved into general-purpose technologies, their products have become increasingly substitutable. As a result, the marketplace has become more competitive, putting downward pressure on prices. 7.2 Impact of Correlated Preferences on Competition Product differentiation is an important source of market power. Although we find substantial heterogeneity in consumers’ overall preferences for AI, there is limited differentiation in their preferences across providers. As shown in panel (c) of Table 3, preferences for AI products are highly correlated. Conditional on how

Conditional on how much a consumer likes AI overall, the consumer tends to have similarly favorable preferences for all AI providers. To illustrate the importance of correlated preferences for competition, Table 5 considers a counterfactual in which preferences are uncorrelated, so the off-diagonal entries ofΣθ are zero. Under this counterfactual, prices would be unambiguously higher in 2026Q1. In particular, all providers modestly increase their prices, with changes ranging from 2.1% for OpenAI, which has the smallest price response, to 8.7% for xAI, which has the largest price response. The directional change in market shares differs across providers. The market shares of Anthropic and xAI increase by 28.8% and 29.8%, respectively , whereas the market shares of OpenAI and GoogleAI decrease slightly—by less than 3%. Intuitively , Anthropic’s preferences are the most strongly correlated with those of the other three providers. Its market share therefore increases substantially when consumers who prefer Anthropic no longer have strong preferences for its competitors. xAI also experiences a sizable increase in market share because preferences for xAI and GoogleAI are highly correlated in the baseline and GoogleAI is cheaper. As a result, GoogleAI exerts substantial competitive pressure on xAI in the baseline, which is removed in the counterfactual. 7.3 Welfare Effects of Entry Our estimates imply that AI products are close substitutes, creating competitive pressure among providers. A central implication is that the presence of an individual provider—even one that is not the market leader—may meaningfully constrain the prices charged by its rivals. To quantify this competitive discipline, we consider a counterfactual in which Anthropic is removed from the market in 2026Q1 and allow the
