To quantify this competitive discipline, we consider a counterfactual in which Anthropic is removed from the market in 2026Q1 and allow the remaining providers to reoptimize their prices. Anthropic is a particularly informative case because it is a close substitute for OpenAI, while its users also have overlapping preferences for xAI and GoogleAI. The counterfactual therefore illustrates how the loss of one provider propagates through equilibrium prices, market shares, and consumer welfare. Panel (a) of Figure 9 shows the effect of Anthropic’s counterfactual exit on equilibrium prices. OpenAI and xAI increase their prices by 2.0% and 1.1%, respectively , whereas GoogleAI changes its price by -4.4%. Thus, removing Anthropic does not uniformly increase the market power of every remaining provider. Instead, its effects depend on the patterns of substitution and preference correlation across products. Although the price responses are modest in magnitude, they are notable given Anthropic’s small market share. As we show below, these price changes also affect paid adoption and contribute meaningfully to the change in consumer surplus. Panel (b) shows that the changes in equilibrium market shares are similarly heterogeneous. Interestingly , OpenAI’s market share changes by -0.7%, even though its closest substitute has been removed from the market. This seemingly counterintuitive result reflects OpenAI’s en- dogenous pricing response. Anthropic’s removal relaxes the competitive constraint on OpenAI, allowing it to raise its price. This price increase more than offsets the direct inflow of consumers who would otherwise switch from Anthropic to OpenAI, causing OpenAI’s equilibrium market share to fall. GoogleAI’s market share also falls, by -7.0%, whereas xAI’s market share increases by 17.1%. xAI’s disproportionate response reflects the distribution of consumers’ preferences for bundling. Although OpenAI and

chunks.text: market share also falls, by -7.0%, whereas xAI’s market share increases by 17.1%. xAI’s disproportionate response reflects the distribution of consumers’ preferences for bundling. Although OpenAI and Anthropic are the most substitutable pair on average, as captured byΓ, the individual-level estimates ofΓfor xAI and Anthropic have very low dispersion. Consequently , most Anthropic users view xAI as a net substitute, and removing Anthropic shifts many of these users toward xAI despite xAI’s higher equilibrium price. GoogleAI and Anthropic, by contrast, are not strong net substitutes. Moreover, xAI’s expansion intensifies competition with GoogleAI because preferences for these two products are highly correlated, reducing GoogleAI’s market power and inducing it to lower its price. Accounting for these supply-side responses is important for evaluating welfare. The direct loss of access to Anthropic understates the total welfare effect because the remaining providers endogenously adjust their prices. In particular, the price increases by OpenAI and xAI amplify the direct welfare loss from removing Anthropic. Panel (c) shows that, when expressed per AI user, removing Anthropic reduces welfare by $5.05 per quarter. This general-equilibrium welfare loss is 21% larger than the partial-equilibrium loss reported in Section 6.2. Overall, the counterfactual demonstrates that competition in the AI market depends not only on the number and market shares of providers, but also on the structure of substitution among their products. Because consumer preferences are highly correlated across providers and AI products are strong substitutes, Anthropic impacts its rivals’ prices even though consumers frequently use multiple products. Removing Anthropic therefore generates welfare losses beyond the direct loss of access to its product, as the pricing responses of the remaining providers amplify the initial harm. 8 Conclusion We document new patterns in consumer demand for paid generative

chunks.text: ond the direct loss of access to its product, as the pricing responses of the remaining providers amplify the initial harm. 8 Conclusion We document new patterns in consumer demand for paid generative AI services. Despite AI’s prominence in public and business discourse, paid consumer adoption remains relatively modest, although it grew rapidly toward the end of our sample. In April 2026, 2.4% of consumers paid for an OpenAI product, making OpenAI the most widely adopted provider. Paid adoption of Anthropic products also increased substantially during the final months of our sample. Adoption is concentrated among younger and higher-income consumers. We also find that paid demand exhibits limited persistence and that multihoming across providers is common, particularly early in the sample, although multihoming has declined over time. Our structural model provides additional insight into these patterns. We estimate substan- tial heterogeneity in consumer preferences, but that preferences for general-purpose AI services are highly correlated across providers. At the same time, the relationship between OpenAI and Anthropic has evolved: the two services have become increasingly substitutable over time. This shift is consistent with the growing overlap in their capabilities. Our supply-side model shows how these demand patterns shape competition. Increasing substitutability and overlap among services intensify price competition. In particular, consumers view services from Anthropic and OpenAI as close substitutes. These competitive forces affect both the total welfare generated by paid AI services and the division of surplus between consumers and providers. The resulting limits on firms’ ability to sustain market power also bear directly on firm valuations throughout the industry . 28
